One of the four resisted and was riddled with bullets. The other three were then hanged to surrounding trees. The posse has sworn to run down all the negroes who fled to the hills on the night of the affray. There are at least fifteen other negroes in hiding.

MORE TROUBLE AND BLOODSHED EXPECTED.

WAHALAK, Miss., December 19.—The trouble between the whites and blacks of this place is not yet settled, and serious trouble and much bloodshed is almost sure to follow. It is known that in the past twenty-four hours two negroes, and perhaps more, have been killed. There is much excitement in town and vicinity. Seventy-five armed men started from here last night, after burying M. H. Maury. The party camped all night at the foot of a low range of hills where the murderers are supposed to be concealed. They believe they have tracked the fugitives, and are to-day advancing on them from all directions. Developments of a bloody character may be expected. Pompey Coleman, who lives in the neighborhood of the trouble, came in last night and reported that Cash Maury and Allen Coleman (negroes), suspected to have been involved in the ambuscade of Sunday, were caught in the swamp last night by the avenging posse and killed. The information is accepted here as authentic, although nothing is known of the manner of their deaths and the disposition of their bodies. Communication with the seat of war is very difficult. A dense swamp separates the hills from Wahalak, and the roads are so bad that travel even on horseback is exceedingly difficult. Something like fifteen negroes are suspected of complicity in Sunday night's affair, and there is no probability of peace until they either escape or are rendered harmless in some other way.

NEW ORLEANS, December 19.—The Pica yune's Wahalak special says: Dick Cheatham and Anthony Wilder have been caught and Zack Maury is under surveillance. Six other negroes are known to be trying to escape on the night trains above here, and the stations are being watched by the pursuers. They cannot escape. The other negroes engaged in the massacres of the whites are not located. There are seven of them. Wilder was captured at a store in Shuqulk. Two loaded guns were found in a barn on his premises. Cheatham was arrested at Mr. L. Jones' house, where he was helping kill hogs. He confessed, and told where six of the fugitives had breakfasted, among them George Maury, the ringleader. They were waiting until night to board a train. The whites distributed themselves along the road accordingly. The prisoners are kept in a frame building ten miles from Wahalak under a strong guard. Their fate will be determined in twenty-four hours. Satisfactory evidence is at hand that the a. bush party consisted of the men led by George Maury. Other members known are Walter Brook, Will Martin alias "Coe," George Coleman, Henry Bush, Dick Cheatham, Anthony Wilder, Cash Maury, John Prince and Andrew Stennis. It is not likely that any of them will get away. The wounded whites are worse to-night, and it is feared three of them will die.
george-maury-wahalak-1888-12-19.A21:
ALL IS QUIET.

The Kemper County Riot Ended.

All the Fugitives, With Three Exceptions, Make Their Escape.

These Three Prisoners Are Said to Be Out of Harm's Way.

At Least, This Is Inferred From What the Guards Say.

Sensational Literature and Inciting Harangues the Cause
Sensational Literature and Inciting Harangues the Cause
Of the Strained Relations Between the Whites and Blacks.
The Thirteen Negroes Who Got Away Will Doubtless Be Content to Remain Absent for Many Moons— There's No Room for Them in Kemper County.
Special from a Staff Correspondent.
WAHALAK, Miss., Dec. 20.—The race troubles of Kemper County are practically at an end for the time being, and affairs are beginning to assume their normal complexion. The armed force of whites which have been scouring the country for nearly ninety-six continuous hours, have been dispersed, and the riotous negroes, with three exceptions, have thus far eluded capture. There were sixteen on the list marked for punishment. Three of them, Dick Cheatham, Anthony Wilder and Zach Maury were captured yesterday, as already reported. The other thirteen have shaken the dust of Kemper from their feet, and are expected to attempt escape by boarding passing trains. News was received today that Walter Crook, George Maury and others of the ring leaders, were heading for Meridian, about forty-eight miles south of here. The trains are watched, however, and vigilant eyes are on the lookout all along the line. It is not likely that the fugitives will show their faces between railroad stations; their safer course is to keep to the woods and push on to points further South. There is a continuous stretch of flat woods extending from Macon, a point twelve miles from here, to Meridian, forty-eight miles South. These woods are covered with a dense growth of trees, and furnish an almost perfect place of concealment to fleeing conspirators. If they stick to the woods their chances of escape are good; whenever they strike a negro cabin they will find friends, food and shelter, and cabins inhabited by white men they are not likely to encounter. The avenging party realizes this thoroughly, and the long and fatiguing horseback chase has been abandoned. The three negroes who were captured last night have doubtless been put out of harm's way, the guards in whose custody the prisoners were left at the White House, report that they got away last night. They recommend, however, that the names of Dick Cheatham, Zack Maury and Anthony Wilder be stricken from the list as unworthy further apprehension. The list has been accordingly so amended and now contains but thirteen names. These Kemper County mountaineers are grim humorists. Further developments today indicate that the flames of race hostility which broke out Sunday night have long been smouldering.

The first firebrand was furnished by a series of letters sent from this State to the Detroit News, Cincinnati Post, Indianapolis Sun and St. Louis Chronicle by one W. H. Hinmans, drawing slanderous pictures of alleged intimidation of negroes and frauds at the polls. Letters were published in the Post and widely circulated among the negroes in this section. Another firebrand was furnished by Gen. W. T. Sherman's article in the October number of the North American Review, entitled "Old Shady." The intimation to that effect thrown out in these dispatches last night at a venture received startling confirmation today. Your correspondent has unimpeachable authority for the statement that on the Sunday preceding the fatal riot, a negro circuit rider of the Methodist Church read Sherman's article from the pulpit of his church in DeKalb, the county seat of Kemper County.

J. Curry, Superintendent of Public Education, is said to have been present, and my informant gave him as authority for the statement. Curry is a white man of excellent repute.

The men of Kemper County seem to have acted with admirable self praise and unusual moderation in view of the strong provocation they had to indiscriminate violence. "Touch not a hair of an innocent man's head" was the Captain's order and it seems to have been sacredly observed. As far as known no property has been destroyed except the accidental destruction by fire of George Maury's residence.

The name Wahalak is likely in a day or two to relinquish its claim to public attention as a news center. The special correspondents leave by an early train tomorrow evening, and the extra force of operators will be withdrawn. If the fugitives turn up anywhere, it is not likely to be in this neighborhood; they doubtless appreciate the fact that their presence will not be tolerated for many days to come. There is little more to say.

Another chapter has been added to the record of blood, which marks distinctive phases of the negro problem—two white men have been killed, three negroes are missing, thirteen negroes are fugitives, and the bottom rail remains where it has been for centuries. HEMMED IN BY AVENGERS.
The Remaining Negro Murderers Have but Little Longer to Live. MERIDIAN, Misc. Dec. 31. The bodies of
The Remaining Negro Murderers Have but Little Longer to Live.

MERIDIAN, Miss., Dec. 21.—The bodies of Maury, Coleman and Davis, lynched by the white avengers, were still hanging to the pine tree near Wahalak yesterday morning. That the trouble has not ended, but will yet result in serious consequences, is known, be cause groups of armed men from Shuqualak, Scooba, Sacarnochee and other towns in the vicinity came into Wahalak to join the armed men already here, who are trying to capture the refugee negroes.

The comparative isolation of the place and difficulty in reaching the scene of the trouble tend to discredit some of the news received. The negroes cannot prevent capture much longer, as the whites believe they have completely shut them in. Coleman, who suffered death, informed his captors of the hiding places of his companions, and the deaths of George Maury, Walter Brook, the two Stennis brothers, Wilder, John Price, Cheatham and the others who are missing is only a question of a few hours.

The wildest reports come from Wahalak about the killing of negroes, but the reports are deemed untrustworthy. It was also said that three of the whites who were wounded in Sunday's massacre had died.

THE RACE WAR.
The Mississippi Negroes Surrounded—Two
The Mississippi Negroes Surrounded—Two Correspondents Depart in a Hurry.

gill-woodward-1888-04.A13:
HORSE THIEVES LYNCHED.
A Deputy Marshal's Posse Has a Severe Battle with Outlaws in No Man's Land.
Kansas Vigilantes Pursue the Desperadoes in Force and Hang Four of Them.
[Oklahoma (Ind. Ter.) special.]
A courier from Shawneetown, forty miles from here, in "No Man's Land," on the North Fork of the Canadian, brings the report of a terrible battle between outlaws and a posse of the United States Marshal which was followed by an uprising of the farmers on the border of Kansas, who meted out summary justice to four horse-thieves and have the rest of the band besieged in the hills.

Three colored horse-thieves stole a bunch of horses from Long Tom, a Shawnee Indian. When the theft was discovered, a Deputy United States Marshal, with a party of Sac and Fox Indian police, gave pursuit and came up with the negro thieves, who at once opened fire upon the officers with Winchesters, anhorsing one policeman at the first round. A regular pitched battle then followed, in which two of the negroes were killed, and one policeman mortally wounded, dying soon after. The Marshal was also badly wounded. The horses were recovered.

When this affair became known a party of fifty ranchmen started for the haunts of the outlaws. They had hardly crossed the line before they were met by a band of the thieves and succeeded in capturing four of them. They were immediately strung up to the nearest tree. The remainder of the band were then so hotly pressed by the avengers that they were compelled to run to earth in a dugout, where they were held at bay when the courier left. It was the intention of the farmers to compel them to surrender by starving them out. There are thought to be six in the dugout, and when captured they will undoubtedly be hanged.

To increase the excitement there are flocking into the Territory quite a number of Oklahoma boomers who firmly believe that this portion of the Territory will soon be open for settlement, and the soldiers are kept continually escorting them back to the State line. There is now being prepared a military map of the Territory to be used by the commanding officers in their scouting in search of the boomers as well as fugitives from justice. Further actions and developments are anxiously awaited.

[Woodward (Ind. Ter.) special.]

A large band of horse-thieves have lately made their headquarters in the neutral strip generally known as "No Man's Land" and have been making frequent raids on the border towns of Southern Kansas, driving off both the cattle and the horses of the farmers. This has so incensed the farmers that they have organized themselves into vigilance committees, determined to rid themselves of this pest. About twenty-five men from the vicinity of Coldwater, Kansas, overtook one of the band named Gill about fifteen miles from this point and shot him. Gill had in his possession at the time he was captured six horses belonging to the members of the vigilance party. Armed parties are continually passing and repassing this point on the lookout for horse-thieves, and if any are caught they will enforce the death penalty without trial.

A Desperado Finally Gets His Dues.
LITTLE ROCK, ARK., April 16.—Alvices from Indian Territory say: Wm. Gill, the notorious horse thief, was shot and killed Friday last-fifteen miles beyond Woodward. Gill has a secluded spot on the bank of the Wasita river where he secreted stolen horses. He has been depredating in Missouri, Arkansas and Kansas. He visited Kansas and secured five horses with the assistance of accomplices, was pursued by over twenty men, among whom were the owners of the animals. He was literally riddled with bullets, as he refused to surrender. He is said to have served two terms in the Kansas State prison. He is said to have stolen in his time five hundred horses.

henry-coleman-norfolk-1888-09-11.A2:
A FIENDISH MURDER.
A Negro Kills James Grant with an Axe-Lyuching Probable if Found. [Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
NORFOLK, VA., September 6.—A shocking—almost double—murder occurred on O'Keefe's farm, on the Indian-Poll bridge, a few miles from the city, this afternoon about 4 o'clock. A negro laborer entered the stable of James Grant, a dairyman, and, watching his opportunity, attacked him with an axe and split open his skull and killed him instantly. The murderer then hid the body under a lot of hay and manure and went to the house and informed Mr. Grant's housekeeper, a Mrs. Reed, that Old-Man Grant was lying drunk under a hay-pile in the stable. He then attacked her with the axe, striking her on the head, and left her, as he supposed, dead, and robbed the house of all the money he could find, a gun and a pistol, and some clothing, and made off to the country. The housekeeper revived sufficiently to crawl out to the road to give the alarm, and soon after the body was found at the stable. The police are now after the negro, and think he is one formerly a driver for the deceased named Coleman, who was discharged by him recently. A lynching is probable if the negro is apprehended very soon. Justice A. W. Hawks held an inquest. The deceased was also keeper of the Catholic cemetery and much respected in the neighborhood.
henry-coleman-norfolk-1888-09-11.A4:
GRANT'S MURDERER CAPTURED.
The Norfolk County Fiend Arrested at Cape Henry--Vessels Ashore.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
Nevada, VA. September 10. About

[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

NORFOLK, V.A., September 10. About 3 o'clock to-day Chief-of-Police Rolland received a message stating that a negro had been arrested by a county constable near Cape Henry with two revolvers on his person, and a description of Coleman was wanted. A description of the murderer was at once telegraphed, and the answer came back that the man under arrest filled the bill and to send an officer down for him. The Chief detailed Captain Mordecai and Officer Prince and they left on the 4 o'clock train over the Virginia Beach railroad. About 9 o'clock to-night the officers and the sheriff of Princess Anne returned to the city with Coleman and lodged him safely in jail. He was captured by two negroes and turned over to the sheriff. He made a full confession of the murder of the old man, James Grant, to the sheriff. A crowd of over three hundred people met the officers
henry-coleman-norfolk-1888-09-11.A5: A MOB AFTER A MURDERER.—In Norfolk early yesterday morning a mob of whites and blacks made an effort to lynch the negro, Henry Coleman, in jail there charged with murdering dairyman James Grant. The crowd, with their faces concealed by handkerchiefs and masks, made an attack upon the station-house, but were easily repulsed and kept at bay by the police. The only result was the breaking of the glass in the station-house doors, but they could not force an entrance. The police stood with drawn revolvers, but did not find it necessary to fire a shot. Two of the rioters were captured by the police and locked up, and Mayor Banks being summoned addressed the mob, which numbered about 300 people, and urged them to disperse, stating that in the case of the prisoner the law will be fully vindicated. His remarks were received with cheers and the crowd gradually dispersed. At five o'clock yesterday morning Coleman, in charge of a strong detail of police, was quietly taken out by the rear entrance, and met by a detachment of the Norfolk City Guard, which had been summoned, and taken to the county jail in Portsmouth, where a dense crowd was attracted. Fearing an attack, the Old Dominion Guards of that city were ordered out to guard the jail, thirty rounds of ammunition being issued to each man. During the attack attack yesterday morning upon the Norfolk jail there were only five men on duty. The mob first cut the rope of the alarm bell to prevent the giving of a general alarm, but they could not face the muzzles of five revolvers in the doorway. The police captured several masks, a sledge hammer and two ropes with rough slip knots at the end of each. The county jail is well guarded, though there is no telling how soon there may be trouble.
henry-coleman-norfolk-1888-09-11.A6:
A MADDENED MOB
ATTEMPTS TO LYNCH THE MURDERER COLEMAN AT PORTSMOUTH.
The Military Ordered Out-A Mob Makes a Rush for the Station-House-Re-pulsed by Police, Etc.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.1

Norfolk, September 11.—A tremendous excitement was created in Portsmouth this morning by the arrival of Henry Albert Coleman, the negro murderer of James Grant, the dairyman, back of Norfolk. One half the town, white and black, turned out and visited the vicinity of the jail, expecting to get a glimpse of the murderer or see some sort of demonstration. The prisoner was carried over from Norfolk in the custody of Chief-of-Police Rolland and his assistants and sixteen officers, surrounded by the Norfolk City Guard, and was met at the wharf in Portsmouth by Chief-of-Police Tynan and a squad of men. Over a hundred people followed the procession from Norfolk and the throng swelled considerably larger by the time the jail was reached, on the corner of Washington and High streets. The military drew up in front of the jail entrance and the prisoner was quickly hustled into the dungeon. All this imposing parade was necessary to provide against the threats of the mob to lynch the prisoner and the manifest desire to get at him. To insure the delivery of the prisoner to the Norfolk county authorities he was handcuffed to two Norfolk policemen, so that it was impossible to have dragged him away. Sheriff Bunting, of the county, was informed that a mob was organizing in Huntersville to assault the jail and he at once applied to Mayor J. Thompson Baird, of Portsmouth, to order out the military of the city, which was promptly done, and the Old Dominion Guard, under command of Captain James M. Binford, have been patrolling Portsmouth all day. At noon Justice A. W. Hawks, of Huntersville, visited the jail and had the prisoner brought before him in the office, and he was formally committed for ten days. Unless Judge Parker orders a special grand jury term of the County Court the prisoner will not be tried until December.

Among a certain class in Norfolk there was great excitement nearly all night, and about half-past 1 o'clock this morning an attempt was made to take the murderer from the station-house and lynch him. A mob of about seventy-five persons, young men and boys, some with colored handkerchiefs over their faces for masks, made a rush on the entrance to the station, but the detachment of police fought them back and repulsed them with their billies and then stood with drawn revolvers. After a short struggle the mob retired before the determined front of the police, and with sticks and stones smashed in every window-glass in front of the station-house. At 2 o'clock Mayor R. G. Banks appeared on the scene and addressed the rioters in a conciliatory speech, appealing for a submission to the laws. The speech had a good effect, and the mob gave three cheers for the Mayor and dispersed. Sergeant Mordecai was hurt by flying fragments of glass. Two of the foremost rioters, young men named Brown and Holland, who had their faces concealed, were captured by the police, and this morning Police-Justice Baum sent them on to court for trial. Everything is now quiet, though a large throng of people linger around the jail in Portsmouth, and it is not probable there will be any further demonstration. The military will remain on duty all night, however, in Portsmouth. The murderer in his confession tells the manner in which he killed his victim with an axe, and says he did so because Mr. Grant owed him money and would not pay it. He says he did not intend to kill Mrs. Louisa Spratt.

Colonel H. C. Hudgins, commanding the Fourth regiment of Virginia volunteers, to-day telegraphed Governor Lee that the Mayor of Portsmouth had made requisition upon him for troops to guard the jail against any violence, and that he had ordered out one company and would send more if necessary. Governor Lee immediately sent the following reply:

"Colonel H. C. Hudgins, Commanding Fourth Virginia Regiment, Norfolk, Va.:

"Dispatch received. The negro Coleman now in jail in Portsmouth must be protected from violence if it takes all the troops under your command.

FITZHUGE LEE."
henry-coleman-norfolk-1888-09-11.A12:
NORFOLK COMING TO RICHMOND.
That is, the county will Make Exhibit—Numerous Norfolk Notes.
[Correspondence of the Richmond Dispatch.]
Nevada September 19, 1898

NORFOLK, September 12, 1888.

The Board of Supervisors of Norfolk county has made an appropriation of $500 to make an exhibit of the resources of the county at the Richmond Exposition. A number of the large farmers of the county, Mr. George A. Wilson, and others, will make individual exhibits.

The Merchants and Manufacturers' Exchange of this city will shortly take action looking to the suitable representation of Virginia's seaport at the Exposition.

The recent eight days of bad weather completely destroyed the truckers' hay crop and considerable millet and fodder. The hay was shocked in the fields when the rain set in and it all rotted. The truckers will all have to buy provender this season.

The troops on duty at the county jail in Portsmouth were withdrawn to-day, but will be stationed there again tonight, as Sheriff Bunting believes that all danger of an assault on the jail and the lynching of the murderer Coleman is not yet over. Fifty men were on duty last night, a detail of ten being sent to the jail every two hours from the armory at the City Hall. The prisoner now converses very freely about the murder and says if old man Grant had paid him what he owed him he would not have killed him. He says he is not afraid of being lynched, and it is hardly probable he will be.

Correspondence of the Yorkville Enquirer.
AN ATROCIOUS OUTRAGE.

CATAWBA JUNCTION, December 3.—On last Wednesday morning, between eight and nine o'clock, little Helen Abernathy, daughter of Mr. W. C. Abernathy, was brutally assaulted by a black fiend named Jack Barnett.

The circumstances of the horrible affair are as about follows: Little Helen and her brother and sister, Charlie and Mittie, aged four and six years respectively, were on their way to their grand mothers's house, about two miles from their own home, on the G., C. & N Railroad. When the children were about half way, they were met by the negro who tried to entice them down into the railroad cut, along the side of which the foot path run; telling them that there was a "pretty snake with a rattle on it down there." The children were frightened and attempted to run away, but the negro seizing Helen, the oldest, threw her down into the cut—twelve feet deep—and then going down to where she was, attempted to accomplish his horrible purpose. The cries of the little brother and sister on the bank attracted to the spot some negro women who were picking cotton in a neighboring field. At their approach, the negro ran away from his intended victim, leaving her in an almost unconscious condition. The child had been almost suffocated in the brute's attempt to stifle her cries, and her arm had been severely sprained by her fall into the cut.

Pursuit was organized as soon as possible and Barnett was followed to Lancaster, fifteen miles distant, where he was captured on Thursday morning by Messrs. Sep Massey, T. M. Allen and John Lindsay. He was hurried away from town just in time to escape lynching, and brought back to this place to find another large party discussing the same purpose. The law abiding spirit of the Junction people prevailing, however, the negro again escaped his merited punishment, and was taken to Yorkville by way of the Three C's Railroad and lodged in jail on Thursday night by Messrs. Sep Massey and J. W. Roddey.

Barnett was identified by the children and made a full confession of the whole affair. He is a thick set, black negro, about five feet high and seventeen years of age.

A Lynching Threatened at Any Moment.
COLUMBIA, S.C., December 10.—Jack Barnett is in the Yorkville jail and may be lynched at any moment. On Thursday evening, little Helen Bernatheck, ten years old, and her brother and sister, four and six respectively, were passing through the woods going home, when Barnett, a powerful negro, met them and tried to get the party to go with him. The children started to run when Barnett caught Helen and threw her down an embankment. He followed and after almost strangling her to death assaulted her. The screams of the other children soon brought some negro women to the scene and Barnett was driven away. Then he was pursued by white men and captured twenty miles away.
He and his captors were followed by a lynching party but he was landed safely in jail. Another lynching party afterwards organized but was dispersed.

TOOK LAUDANUM. DELIBERATE SUICIDE OF A YOUNG MAN IN LYNCHBURG. Prepared Himself for Burial—His Letter to the Hotel Proprietor—Escaped Lynching. [Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
LYNCHBURG, VA., December 28.—Robert Hull, brother of Allen G. Hull, travelling passenger agent of the Norfolk and Western railroad, was found dead in Room No. 44 at the Norvell-Arlington Hotel this morning. He arrived at the hotel Saturday night and registered as "Robert Moore, city." Mr. Davis, the clerk, was in his room on Sunday and chatted with him for a short while. He seemed to be in good spirits, but complained of being a little unwell. Davis suggested sending for a physician, but Hull said it was not necessary. He remained in his room all day yesterday and refused to admit the colored employees who called to see if he wanted anything, saying if he wanted anything he would let them know. Hull not putting in an appearance at the breakfast-table this morning the colored porter went up and knocked at the door. He received no response, and on going again with a like result he shoved the key, which was on the inside, out of the lock and opened the door. Mr. Davis was with the porter on the second visit, and finding the young man dead, reported the fact to Mr. Stockton Terry, the proprietor, who, upon going to the room, found the following letter sealed:

"To Proprietor: I regret having to inconvenience you in this manner, but was compelled to do so. Send a message to Warren L. Rohr, ticket agent of the Norfolk and Western depot, asking where Allen Hull (who is my brother) is located. Should he not know telegraph Allen Hull at Roonoke, Va., and if no answer comes, send a telegram to W. B. Bevill and M. F. Bragg, at the same place, stating the circumstances, &c. My purse, containing $20, you'll find in my veat with my watch and scarf-pin. I have just taken a bath and put on clean clothes, so that will hardly be necessary to go through again. My name is not Moore, but Robert Hull."

The letter was lying on the bureau, and near it was one addressed to his brother, as follows: "Mr. Allen Hull—to be delivered upon his arrival." Near this was a package of cigarettes, while the linen he had removed was on the table.

The dead man was lying on his back with his hands crossed on his breast and a handkerchief spread on his head. He was apparently about thirty years of age, and so strongly resembled his brother that Coroner Busey, who arrived soon thereafter, readily recognized him.

Under the bed were found two two-ounce bottles labelled laudanum. One was empty while about a third remained in the other. In a bureau-drawer was found another empty bottle, which showed that he had taken no less than five ounces.

The coroner's jury gave a verdict of suicide.

Hull had been employed as fireman on the Norfolk and Western railroad, but had not been on duty for some time on account of ill health. One of his friends who is in the city to-day said he had fits of despondency on account of bad health, but he knew no other troubles that would cause him to commit suicide.

Mr. Allen G. Hull, brother of the unfortunate young man, arrived here at 2:25, and received the letter. He was much distressed and said; "Brother gave no reason for the act in his letter. It was simply a good-bye to mother and myself." His remains will be shipped to his old home in Augusta, Ga., tomorrow morning.

THE WRONG MAN SUFFERS FOR A MURDER DONE
IN A DRUNKEN BRAWL.
Corning, N. Y., Sept. 9 (Special).—This afternoon about 5 o'clock John King was shot and killed by an Italian laborer, whose name is unknown, in a drunken row about a woman. The murderer and his companions fled toward Knoxville, a village across the river, pursued by officers who arrested one of the men. They were met on the way to Corning by a crowd of several hundred persons. The crowd finally became ungovernable, and charged on the prisoner with clubs and stones, beating him into insensibility. Later another Italian was arrested. Rain prevented the crowd from mobbing him. The woman says that the wounded man is not the one who did the shooting.

MURDER IN CORNING. A Young Irlahman Shot Through the Heart by an Italian in a Saloon Fight.
CORNING, N. Y., Sept. 9.—Three Italian laborers were drinking in John Healy's saloon on West Market street at 5 o'clock this afternoon, when John King entered and joined the Italians at the bar. Soon afterward May Caven, a disreputable weman, came in. She was known to all of the men. Upon her exhibiting tokens of affection toward King the Italians became angry, and a fight ensued, in which one Italian drew an old-fashioned pistol and fired at King, who drepped dead. The bullet had pierced his heart, going through his body. The Italians fled, going toward Knoxville, a village across the river, where a gang of Italian laborers live. Policemen followed them, and after a hot chase ran down one man, who was brought toward Corning. On arriving at the bridge the prisoner was met by a big crowd, who kept up a running fire of threats and calls of "Throw him in the river!" The mob finally became ungovernable. Paving stones and clubs and missiles of every description were hurled at the prisoner, who dropped unconscious to the ground. The crowd was told that he was dead. Then he was picked up, placed in a carriage, and driven to jail and doctors were summoned. The man was terribly hurt. His head was out and one eye partly torn out. Another Italian was arrested in an immoral house in Knoxville and brought to Corning. The rain prevented him from being mobbed. The woman was taken to jail and identified both men as being concerned in the night, but neither one did the shooting. The police are searching for the third man, and he will probably be caught before morning. A large crowd has gone out to search for him. The excitement is everywhere intense, and the streets are crowded. The murdered man was head potmaker in the Corning Glass Works, and was somewhat addicted to drink. He was 25 years old, unmarried, and had lived in Corning six years. His parents live in Ireland. The saloon where the affray took place is one of the worst holes in town. The proprietor is a special policeman himself. The Sunday laws are perfectly ignored here.

DID THE MOB KILL THE WRONG MAN!

Corning, N. Y., Sept. 10 (Special).—Yesterday afternoon pedestrians on West Market-st. were startled by cries of "Murder!" from a saloon in the Goff Block. It was found that an Italian had shot and killed John King, an employee of the Corning Glass Works, while both were drunk. The murderer had been seen to cross the Knoxville bridge, but he gained at least fifteen minutes' start on the officers. The depot policemen, followed by a crowd, then started in pursuit, and arrested an Italian who they found moving rapidly away from the scene of the murder, and whose looks were the more suspicious in that his face was bleeding from several cuts. This man, protesting his innocence, was brought back to Corning, followed by a threatening mob. The mob, catching up stones, pelted the Italian until he dropped senseless. The officers finally pushed their way through the crowd, the unconscious man still receiving blows from sticks and stones, until they reached a livery stable. From there the man was carried in a carriage to the lockup, where he died in a few minutes.

To-night it is rumored that the man killed by the mob was innocent, and that the guilty man has been arrested. John King, the man who was shot, came to this country from Ireland six years ago.

- At Corning, N. Y., Sunday, John King was shot and killed by one of three Italians in a saloon quarrel. Officers caught one Italian and a mob nearly killed him.

- During a cyclone, on Thursday of last week, three large vessels and several smaller crafts were lost near Vera Cruz, Mexico. Considerable other damage was done.

- A Connecticut couple couldn't agree on a physician to attend one of their children, and a squabble which followed now has its outcome in a suit for divorce instituted by the wife.

- A gentleman who refused to have his name made public, entered the New York Mayor's office Tuesday and left his check for $12,000 for the relief of the yellow-fever sufferers at Jacksonville.

- Charles Low was selling snake oil in Columbus, Ga., Saturday night, and during his talk exhibited a rattle snake which bit him on the hand. He made for a drug store, where he fell unconscious and will likely die.

ANOTHER NEGRO OUTRAGE. Louisiana Whites Murder a Law-Abiding Colored Citizen. NEW ORLEANS, July 80.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.—Repeated outrages against the blacks are becoming so serious as to cause thoughts of an exodus. News comes now of a peculiarly brutal piece of lawlessness in Assumption parish, the home of Governor Nicholls. The house of a law-abiding colored man named John Lynn was broken open and entered by a mob of thirty-five armed white men. In the darkness the mob could not see where their victim was stationed, so one of their number was ordered to strike a light. As soon as the light was made, Lynn, from his hiding place in the house, shot and killed the man who made it. The attacking party captured Lynn, and took possession of his home. Leaving several of their number to guard their prisoner and his home, they carried away the dead body of their accomplice and buried him. Returning to Lynn they took him out and shot him to pieces, his body being perforated in no less than twelve places. This act became known all over the parish, but the officers of the law have made no effort to capture the midnight marauders. The colored people are considering a wholesale exodus from the parish on account of the entire withdrawal of the protection of the law from them. IN THE POLITICAL FIELD. J. W. Hustin Reviews the Situation in Indiana. THE GUBERNATORIAL CONTEST. Workingmen Well Posted on the Leading Issues of the Day and Rallying to the Support of Harrison. The Indiana Republicans.
CHICAGO, July 30.—[Special Telegram to THE BEE.—A conference of the chairmen of the republican state committees of Indiana, Wisconsin, Michigan and Illinois, was held this afternoon. Chairman J. W. Huston, of Indiana, said, in regard to the situation in his state. "It is very hopeful."

"Is there trouble in the republican party in Indiana, growing out of the fact of ex-Governor Porter taking the race for governor!"

"I should say none. While Governor Porter was evidently the choice of a majority of Indiana republicans, still I believe that other nominations might be made that would call forth in support of the ticket the greatest possible effort and enthusiasm. The republicans of Indiana have always been free in the expression of their individual preferences before the nominations, but after a nomination has been made they always give a united and determined support to the ticket. Being connected with the party organization, I have felt it rather my duty to look after the organization of the party than attempting to exert any influence in the selection of the party's candidates. It shall be my duty and pleasure in my official connection with the party organization to give my best energies to the election of the ticket, let it consist of whomsoever it may."

"Whom do you expect will head the ticket?"

"There have been a number of gentlemen, for many years leaders of our party in the state, mentioned in connection with the nomination for governor, among whom I would mention the Hon. Will Cumback, of Greensburg; Governor Robertson, of Fort Wayne; Major Steele, of Marion, and the Hon. John M. Butler, of Indianapolis, any of whom would make acceptable candidates to the party generally."

"What is your opinion of the prohibitionists of Indiana at the November election?"

"I feel quite confident that we can carry the state."

"Upon what do you base your opinion?"

"First, because the party generally believes in the necessity of thorough party organization, and because such organization is now being effected in every county in the state. Secondly, because the republicans of Indiana were never more enthusiastic or determined to succeed than at present. We carried the state in 1886, electing our entire state ticket, as the result of party organization, and our organization at this time, in my judgment, is far in advance of what it was at a like period in 1886. While I say that republicans generally are sanguine of success, at the same time their expectations are pre-
judgment, is far in advance of what it was at a like period in 1886. While I say that republicans generally are sanguine of success, at the same time their expectations are predicated upon the assurance of the most thorough party organization and united effort upon the part of all. In fact, I have frequently heard republicans say that we should make this fight in Indiana as thoroughly and vigorously as we would had 20,000 majority to overcome."

"How about this mooted defection of the labor vote as against Mr. Harrison?"

"I think it is greatly exaggerated. The laboring classes in Indiana will not be controlled by misstatements or prejudices, but will thoroughly understand Senator Harrison's attitude toward the laboring classes. They will accord him credit for all he has done in their behalf. While it has been sought diligently to prejudice the laboring men against him, I think it will prove of avail. General Harrison's position on all questions affecting the wage workers of this country has always been that of a true friend, and General Harrison has no more earnest or enthusiastic supporters in the state than such as belong to the laboring classes. Republican clubs, composed wholly of railroad men, are being organized in the railroad centers throughout the state, and they are most enthusiastic in General Harrison's support."

"How about this 'dollar a day for working-men' and Mr. Harrison's Chinese question?"

"Mere bugaboos, such as should be used only to scare children."

—Repented outrages against the blacks in the vicinity of New Orleans are becoming so serious as to cause thoughts of an exodus. News comes now of a peculiarly brutal piece of lawlessness in Assumption parish, the home of Gov. Nicholls. The house of a law-abiding colored man named John Lynn was broken open and entered by a mob of thirty-five armed white men. In the darkness the mob could not see where their victim was stationed, so one of their number was ordered to strike a light. As soon as the light was made, Lynn, from his hiding place in the house, shot and killed the man who made it. The attacking party captured Lynn and took possession of his home. Leaving several of their number to guard their pri-oner and his home, they carried away the dead body of their accomplice and buried him. Returning to Lynn they took him out and shot him to pieces, his body being perforated in no less than twelve places. This act became known all over the parish, but the officers of the law have made no effort to capture the midnight maudrants. The colored people are considering a wholesale exodus from the parish on account of the entire withdrawal of the protection of the law from them.

—Reports of the trouble on the San Carlos reservation in Arizona show that the Indians have been stealing cattle and preparing a supply of dried meat preparatory, it is presumed, to an outbreak. When the party went to arrest the hostiles they were fired upon and three Indian scouts killed. The po so returned fire, wounding several of the band, which immediately left the reservation, followed afterwards by others, all going toward the mountains. All the troops of the various forts in that vicinity are being held in re diness to march sh uld a general outbreak occur.

—The steamship Villa Verde, from Santiago de Cuba, says a New York special, brings the full tidings of the fires that swept Port Au Prince, the capital of Hayti, on the 4th and 7th of July. The fire commenced in the chamber of the deputies on the afternoon of July 4, the boleoni s and outside passages upstairs having been set on fire. From that point it burned down to the rue d arsenal, sweeping away three square blocks of buildings. This fire destroyed that part of the city used largely for private residences. Among them were many valuable and imposing edifices. It is now known that the fire of both days destroyed some 850 buildings, causing a loss of $2,000,000. The fire of July 7th was another section of the arsenal district. During the afternoon it was started in four different localities practically at the same instant. It seems to be more than coincident that the burned district should be the section occupied by the adherents of Gen. Manigat and Senator Legitime, who started the insurrectionary movement of May 17, 1880, and who have been expelled. They

were too dangerous for President Solomon to shoot, and he sent them off but it is said that their petty adherents were crowded into prison. It is be eved that Solomon's own party fired that section to please him

WASHINGTON BRIEFs.

Some members of the Cherokee legislature are in Washington with the avowed intention of preferring charges against R. L. Owen, Indian agent at Muggee, Indian Territory, the largest Indian agency in the United States. It is said he has attempted to dispossess certain cattle companies in the territory to get their leases for o her comp nies in which he is inter- ted. Charges are now said to be pending in the interior department nt. brought by Owen against President Hewit and Attorney Lyon, of the Cherokee Strip Live Stock association, who, he claims, brought whisky into the territory to influence the Indians during the last session of the Cherokee legislature.

Senator Palmer, speaking of his anticipated retirement from public life, said: "No matter how just or upright a public man may be he is always under some suspicion of wrong-doing. We hear a great deal about lobbying. The only lobbying I have ever seen done in congress is legitimate and open. I have waited patiently these five years for somboly to approach me with a bribe or a threat, or an improper request for legislation, but neither the one nor the other have ever come."

Signor Mereno, who has been for years an active opponent of the Italian padron system, has written a letter to the king of Italy accusing Italian consuls in this country of aiding in the contract labor system, and announcing his intention of making these charges before the immigration investigating committee.

Senator Culom has introduced a bill in the house to appropriate $75,000 for a public building at Galesburg, Ill.

In regard to the report in circulation that his tariff speech was set up and published from a "rat" office. Speaker Carlisle says: "I have not seen the statement, but have been informed that such a charge has been made. There is no truth in the statement. Five hundred copies of my speech on the tariff were ordered to be printed at the government printing office, and I have no connection with any order or contract for their publication. If they have been published at any other place, it was done by somebody, on his own responsibility, and without my knowledge, and I am not responsible for it."

Representative Wheeler, of Alabama, recently introduced a bill in the house directing the superintendent of the eleventh census to ascertain and publish the birth and death rate among the pure whites and among the negroes, Chinamen, Indians, half breeds or hybrids of any description or character of the human race who are found in the United States, as well as of mulattos, quindroons and octoroons.

Representative Sowden reported favorably his bill appropriating $70,000 for a public building at Allentown, Pa. The report, after giving a number of statistics to show the importance of the business interests of the town, says that the bill is intended to meet the president's objections to the former bill.

THEY WANTED TO LYNCH HIM.
Socialist Chase Policeman Slater, Believing He Had Shot Their Friend.

CHICAGO, March 4.—All day long the people of Jefferson, a suburb of the city, were in a fever of excitement. Early in the morning Wenzel Cap, a well-known Bohemian saloon keeper, was shot, and fatally wounded, under mysterious circumstances. Wenzel Cap's saloon is a long, one-story building in a sparsely settled portion of Jefferson.

Back of the saloon is a dance hall and back of that the rooms where Capt lived with his wife and children. The saloonkeeper and his family, were up early to prepare for a busy Sunday's work. Cap went into the saloon about 5:30 o'clock in the morning, and less than half an hour later two shots were heard by the family. A twelve-year-old son of the saloonkeeper ran through the dance hall into the saloon, and found it apparently empty.

He stood still a moment, and heard a low moan, apparently coming from beneath the bar. Peering about, he found the body of his father, half buried in the sawdust. Blood was oozing from a ragged hole in the back of his head, his face was terribly scratched and bruised, and his clothes were torn, as it in a struggle. The boy raised his father upon his arm, and found he was still conscious. Cap opened his eyes and said feebly:

"Slater. Slater; get Slater!"

John Slater is the one-armed policeman who patrols the territory about the saloon and usually goes off duty about 6 in the morning. The boy waited for no more, but ran to the door and commenced screaming at the top of his voice. Men and women ran up from all directions, and all were told that Policeman Slater had just shot and killed the saloon keeper. The statement was received without question, and a search through neighboring sheds and probable hiding places was begun.

In less than an hour an infuriated mob was formed. It was composed of the people of the neighborhood, who are Socialists. The wounded Bohemian saloon keeper was popular among them, and besides, they hate the police.

About 8 o'clock Slater was taken in charge by a brother officer. The thoroughly angry crowd saw the bluecoats in a buggy, and as a woman exclaimed "There the murderer comes," a patrol wagon with the dying saloon keeper turned the corner. The sight further maddened them. They started up Oglesby street to meet the buggy. Women had clubs in their hands; men stones and sticks and some revolvers. They also procured a rope and started to Lynch Slater.

The approach of the noisy, threatening mob, and the cries of "Lynch him," warned the Lieutenant not to drive any further. He wheeled his buggy around only a few hundred feet from the crowd and started back. The horse was fiercely lashed and the prisoner was safely landed at West North Avenue station. A posse of officers was at once sent to scatter the mob, but found it had already dispersed.

The would-be lynchers left a strong clothes-line behind. Later developments wholly exonerate Policeman Slater. The detectives are looking for James Posters, who was implicated in the murder. Slater was at home in bed when the shooting occurred. The thought in the dying man's mind undoubtedly was that he wanted the policeman to look for the murderer.

Minnie Teppe's Sad Death. CHARLESTON, S. C., Mar. 4.—Miss Minnie Teppe, the young woman who was the alleged victim of the Langley drugging and raping outrage, died this morning at 9 o'clock. She has been in a half paralyzed and unconscious condition since the exposure of the case. The affair has caused a profound sensation here. BOHEMIANS RUN WILD. An Excited Chicago Mob Want to Lynch an Innocent Man.
CHICAGO, Mar. 4.—An innocent man barely escaped lynching this morning at the hands of an excited mob in the Bohemian district, northwest of the city limits. Wenzel Cap, a saloon keeper, was found by his 12-year old son dying behind the bar. The saloon keeper had been shot and terribly pounded. "Father, father," cried the boy bending over him, "Who has hurt you? Who shot you?" Cap opened his eyes and said feebly, "Slater," "Slater," "Get Slater." The policeman on that beat is named Slater. The boy ran out screaming that his father had been murdered by Slater. Several hundred Bohemian women and children quickly gathered, and providing themselves with clubs, stones, and a long rope started for Slater's house. They had been preceded by a police lieutenant, who was that moment coming toward the mob in a buggy with Slater under arrest. An exciting chase between the mob and the officers began and lasted half a mile, sections of the Bohemians cutting across lots and hurling volley after volley of stones and sticks at the policemen. Slater and the lieutenant at last reached the station-house in safety, and subsequent developments showed that Slater was home in bed when the saloon keeper was attacked, the murderer being a tough named James Potter, who was caught by Cap robbing the saloon till. Cap's dying exclamation was a request to send for the policeman, Slater, not, as the boy supposed, to arrest him as a murderer.

A VOTE OR A LIFE IN ARKANSAS.
SIXTEEN MEN KILLED IN UNION COUNTY.
PREMEDITATED MURDER OF NEGROES AT THE POLLS-DEATH AND DISFRANCHISEMENT AT THE MUZZLE OF A GUN.
AT THE MUZZLE OF A GUN.

St. Louis, Sept. 12 (Special).—A dispatch from Little Rock says: "A reign of terror has succeeded the election outrages in Union County. Eldorado is the county seat. There is neither railroad nor telegraph in Union, Camden and Magnolia. The nearest railroad points are in adjoining counties. The statement of what has occurred in Union County was obtained from responsible white citizens of the county who have just come from there. The week before the election the Democrats visited and wrecked the printing office from which the union labor newspaper had been issued up to that time. On the Saturday night before the election they called upon the leading colored men who were going to vote for Norwood, and warned each one that if he persisted in voting on Monday he would be whipped or killed. To show that they were in earnest the Democrats took out twenty-five negroes representing nearly all of the precincts in the county and flogged them. On Sunday they went to a colored church, killed one negro and wounded several. At 6 o'clock Monday morning 100 white men armed with guns and pistols assembled at Eldorado to direct the election. By the time the polls opened they had killed one negro and whipped another so severely that he will probably die. Whenever a negro came in sight they would ride up to him and punch him with a gun, and warn him off with insulting epithets. This kind of work was kept up all day. When it was over the white men who had been witnesses to the outrages and were known to oppose such things were visited and at the muzzle of a gun were made to promise that they would not prosecute any of the perpetrators.

"Another Union County white man who is here trying to make arrangements to leave there permanently says: 'Every road to Eldorado was guarded with armed men on election day. As the negroes came in they were met and driven back. Unless they struck a trot homeward they were shot or whipped. Jordan Gray was made to pull off his shirt and was then pounded with guns and prodded with the bayonets. He is in bed now. It was reported when I left the county that sixteen persons had been killed since Sunday evening. You never saw so many scared people. A negro was killed at Lisbon on election day. At Champaignolle the ballot box was stolen by the Democrats at noon."

POLITICAL OUTRAGES IN ARKANSAS.
POLITICAL OUTRAGES IN ARKANSAS. NEGROES DRIVEN FROM THE POLLING PLACES. AND THE POLLING BOOKS STOLEN
NEGROES DRIVEN FROM THE POLLING PLACES, AND THE POLLING BOOKS STOLEN.

St. Louis, Sept. 16 (Special).—The feeling over the election outrages grows rather than subsides. Arkansas is indeed thoroughly aroused. Many of her best men believed that the transition from "staff-outs" to honest elections must be accomplished quietly by the gradual growth of a better sentiment. They were mistaken. Something was needed thoroughly to startle the popular conscience. That something was supplied last week by the outrages without parallel in the political history of the State. And now the revolution is fairly under way. Every mail adds details to the story of the outrages in Union County, on the southern border of the State. A letter just received by Secretary Cooper of the Republican State Central Committee says that when the candidates for county offices started around the county the Bourbons would hiss and insult the Reformers and Union Labor party men. After one week's campaigning the Union Labor party and Reformers withdrew from speaking in joint discussion. On Saturday, September 1, Norwood and Eagle spoke at El Dorado. Everything was remarkably quiet. But on Saturday night the marauding and whipping of colored men began. Wherever the Democrats thought that the whipping of some influential colored man would scare the rest of the neighborhood, they did it. Press Neal, a colored man living eight miles north of El Dorado, was severely whipped because he said he would vote as he pleased. Sandy Newton and Aaron Cobb, colored, of different townships, were whipped.

On Monday morning, before daylight, all roads leading to El Dorado were guarded by the militia. They drove all the colored men back and told them to go home and not to come back to town that day. If they did, they would be killed. Some of them went by a by-way and were shot at. Some were visited at their homes and beaten with the guns. Some that were in El Dorado were forced to vote the Bourbon ticket. Even some few white men were told to go home.

The Democratic Canvassing Board has counted in the Democrats in Pulaski County, where the poll books were stolen. The Democratic afternoon paper, "The Arkansas Democrat," says to-day:

It matters not who is guilty of the theft of the poll books from the County Clerk's office. The Democratic party must bear the responsibility. To clear itself of this responsibility, the only way to do it is for the party to refuse to profit by the burglary. If, as is generally believed, the stolen votes will elect the entire Republican ticket, they must be counted for that ticket if the Democracy of Pulaski County would escape all responsibility on account of the robbery. It is not a question of a few offices, but one that is far reaching and overshadowing in its importance, affecting all parties and the rights of every citizen. The Democratic party is in power in Pulaski County, and it cannot profit by this outrage. There is but one way out of the trouble, and that is to spurn all advantages that technicalities might give, and count the votes as they were cast, regardless of the ticket elected.

An attempt was made Monday night to burn the railroad shops at Contocook, by setting fire to waste. The damage is not large.

Policeman Edward H. Murphy, of Brooklyn, was stabbed to death by Henry May, yesterday, because the officer refused to release a prisoner. May was arrested.

The New York Press publishes a letter from R. B. Lee of St. Louis, which says he has just returned from Arkansas, where he took part in the Union Labor party campaign. The Democrats, it is alleged, stole the ballot-box at townships which gave Union Labor majorities, and shot and killed many voters of that ticket. At Eldorado, the county seat of Union county, they took the poll books away from the judges and burned them, and then held a new election, at which no Union Labor man was permitted to vote.

That the election in Arkansas on the 3d inst. was attended with more or less disturbance was briefly noted in the telegraphic returns on the following day. The Union Labor party failed to carry the State, and but little was said about the means used by the Democrats to defeat it. A letter from Mr. R. B. Carl Lee, a prominent leader of the Union Labor party and its principal candidate for Congress two years ago, contains a story of murder, outrage and fraud so startling that it is almost incredible. The letter was received in this city yesterday, and it is as follows:

"St. Louis, Mo., Sept. 14.

"G. W. Pike, New York City:

"Dear Sir and Brother—I am just from Arkansas. If the people of the United States only knew half how we have been treated Congress would wipe out the fraudulent State government in Arkansas and grant us a republican form of government as guaranteed by the federal Constitution.

"In Arkansas county they robbed us of the ballot-boxes at two townships with over 500 majority for us. In Union county Governor Hughes armed the Democratic clubs with the State Winchesters on the night before the election (Sunday). They paraded over the county and whipped over twenty colored men, some of them so badly that they had to keep their beds. On Monday they shot and killed seven white Union Labor men and wounded over twenty more, and at Eldorado, the county-seat, they took the poll books away from the judges and burned them before the eyes of the people and then held a new election at which no Union Labor man was permitted to vote.

"In Miller county the Democratic clubs were armed by Governor Hughes with the State's arms, and they went to the strong Union Labor precincts and notified them that if they voted the Union Labor ticket they would kill them. In Woodruff county they added over 1,000 votes to the Democratic vote, and defrauded us out of the election. In Crittenden county we had over 2,000 majority, this they cut down to less than 250. A delegation of white Wheelers immediately went to Little Rock and waited on Governor Hughes, giving him the facts, but he refused to take any action in the matter.

"In Lee county we had over 2,300 majority; this they counted for our opponents. In Mississippi county they changed 500 votes in the same way. In St. Francis county, at Blackfish, they stacked their guns around the voting place and refused to let the Union Labor people vote. At another township there they stuffed the ballot-box, and refused to let our men vote, when one of our men fired on them with squirrel shot, slightly wounding four of them. This is the only act of violence we are accused of in the State. I am sorry for this one.

"In Jackson county they secretly swindled us out of over 1,000 votes. In Lincoln county they changed over 500 of our votes to them. In Howard county the same. In Lafayette county they stole over 400 votes from us by throwing them out. In Little River county they stole from 500 to 800 votes from us by counting us out. In Garland county about the same number in the same way. In Saline county they stole over 400 votes from us by changing. In Lonoke county, Eaglis's home, they refused to count Williams township, that gave us 352 majority. In Pope county they changed 400 or 500 votes, perhaps more, from our candidate to their candidate. In Conway county they stole 700 or 800 in the same way.

"In Monroe county, at Pine Ridge, they forced the negroes to vote the Democratic ticket, saying: 'This is the ticket you have got to vote today.' In Pulaski county, the county in which Little Rock is situated, they stole nine ballot-boxes and refused to count two others—a loss to us of over 3,000 votes. Besides this, they changed the votes in many of the other wards, so that they gave them, instead of us, a majority.

"We undoubtedly carried the State and have been counted out. Our candidates are contesting, but I fear we can do nothing but show to the world the fraud that has been committed in a legal way, because the same fraud that gave them the State also gave them the Legislature; and it has to be tried before that body. You can use this letter as you see fit. Mind that it is not the Republicans that have been counted out, but the Union Labor ticket. The Republicans counted the Democrats out while they were in power, and now the Democrats count everybody out that is opposed to them. They have armed the Democratic clubs and made militia companies of them. No matter what our strength may be, we can never get it counted until the general government forces them to give us an honest election.

"Until then the shotgun and Winchester rifle in the hands of Democratic clubs and backed by the State officials (and they are backed by the United States government), rule in Arkansas, and not the people. Yours fraternally,

"R. B. CARL LEE."

How Arkansas Was Carried.
Fuller information just received.
How Arkansas Was Carried.

Fuller received, says the New York Mail and Express, confirms all that had been suspected about the way Arkansas was carried for Gov. Eagle by the Democrats. Crittenden county went Democratic for the first time since the war, showing a "change" of 3,000 votes—a change produced by banishing all the prominent negroes, including the county judge, the county clerk and other important officials; by whipping two dozen negroes and serving notice on the rest that they would attempt to vote on peril of their lives, and by intimidation and violence at the polls. Pulaski county was "carried," after a Republican majority of 2,000 had been polled, by breaking into the county clerk's office at Little Rock and stealing the returns from nine Republican precincts. This theft has been badly denounced by Gov. Hughes and other Democratic officials, but no efforts have been made to find out the perpetrators.

Union county, on the southern border of the state, a region in which there is not a single railway, was carried by the most open violence. The Union Labor newspaper office at the county seat, El Dorado, was wrecked the week before election. Negroes were stripped and whipped. A colored church was entered and one negro was killed, another mortally wounded, and still others severely injured. A correspondent of the Globe Democrat, who has been of his information from responsible white citizens of Union county, thus describes the scene at one of the polling places: "In Champagnole precinct, state militia, which had been organized after the militia, which had been organized after the polls and formed two lines. Every voter had to march up to the polls between the ranks of armed men. This was one of the precincts which would have given Norwood a large majority. About noon the Norwood ticket had, according to the tally, 102 ahead of the Democratic ticket. At this time three men with their heads covered with bandana masks marched up to the polls between the two lines of armed men, seized the ballot-box, marched back between the militia ranks and proceeded to destroy the box and its contents, no one molesting them. When the bandana Ku klux first laid hold of the box at the polling place, one of the judges of election resisted. The Ku klux drew a pistol, put it to the judge's head and soon quitted him. When the masked men got beyond the militia line they fired their guns and proceeded to destroy the box. After this episode the Democrats opened another poll, at which only Democrats voted. the Democrats opened another poll, at which only Democrats voted. That night Mr. Cook, a merchant, an old Confederate and one of the leading citizens of Champagne, who had been an avowed supporter of Norwood, had his store and all his goods burned. A majority of about 500 was given Eagle, where there would have been a majority of at least 200 for Norwood with a free ballot and a fair count.

Further testimony is furnished by the Democratic organ at the state capital, the Little Rock Gazette, which prints a despatch from Arkansas county, saying: "Last night we had the disgraceful scene of eight heavily armed men escorting the ballot box in Prairie Township. They swore they would have the stolen box of Old River counted or have blood, but when they saw the determined stand of the Democrats they failed to put their threat into execution. The official count today gives Eagle a majority of 332 over Norwood. The whole state and county Democratic ticket are elected by a small majority, this by leaving out Old River Township, which is strongly Wheeler. The Wheeler will contest. Brickell, Democrat, received a majority of 43 over Langston, Republican, in this county for state senator. Everything quiet.

This Old River box was taken in charge by one Mr. T. L. Krier, who started for the county seat with it. He was stopped on the way by three masked men who took the ballot box from him, and it has never been heard from since. There was about 310 majority for the Republican-Wheeler candidates in the box. Without the votes of this township, the returns show a Democratic majority in the county of from 116 to 150.

HE PAID THE PENALTY.
A Deputy Sheriff Lynched for an Unprovoked Murder.

WAHPETON, DAK., July 27.—Miss Mollie Korbel was shot and killed by Deputy Sheriff L. Slemmer Wednesday evening. No provocation was given for the deed, and the populace became enraged and all last evening the town was filled with angry farmers and citizens, who threatened lynching. At 2 o'clock this morning a masked mob of about 100 men overpowered Sheriff Miller and Deputy Bronte and took the murderer out. They carried him to the bridge over the Bois de Sioux River, and after asking if he wished to pray, and receiving the reply, "No," he was strung and left to hang until daylight this morning. The sheriff did all he could to prevent the lynching, but would not fire on the lynchers, who were all his friends.

HANGED BY A MOB.
The Wahpeton Woman Murderer Taken From Jail and Lynched. Special to the Globe.
The Wahpeton Woman Murderer Taken From Jail and Lynched. Special to the Globe.

WAHPETON, Dak., July 27.—At 1 o'clock this morning a force of 100 masked men attacked the jail, breaking open the outside doors, which admitted them into the lobby where were arrayed Sheriff Miller, Deputy Pelham and a large force of special deputies, for the purpose of repelling any attempt to lynch L. S. Elmer, who had the day before deliberately murdered Miss Mollie Korbel, out of jealousy and cussedness. About the time the sledgehammer party reached Elmer's cell it was noticed that he was

ATTEMPTING TO HANG HIMSELF with a piece of rope, and before he could be reached and cut down he had become quite black in the face. Failing this time he was removed to the opposite side, but was cut down more readily this time. During the fifteen minutes the sledge hammer and chisel experts did their work deftly and Elmer was finally led out of his cell with the noose about his neck and hurried down to the Red river bridge, where he expressed no regrets at his crime, but said he did it and was glad of it, and was at once strung up, watchers being left on the bridge till between 4 and 5 o'clock, when Undertaker Rice cut the body down and Buried It To-Day.

There were probably 800 people in front of the jail fifteen minutes after operations began and as the party passed from door to door this great crowd sent up cheer after cheer.

The funeral of Miss Korbel occurs Saturday forenoon at St. Adelbert's church and in obedience to the sense of a paper passed about the city to-day, it is declared that in honor of the memory of this lovely girl the business houses be closed for the morning.

AN ATROCIOUS MURDER. A Satoka Sheriff Shoots a Female Servant.
Wahpeton, Dak., July 26.—Deputy Sheriff L. S. Elmer murdered Miss Mollie Korbell Wednesday night under circumstances of peculiar atrocity. She was a domestic in the Sheriff's employ, and had been entrusted with the management of the household during the temporary absence of the family. She had just given the prisoners their supper when Elmer, who boarded in the house, asked her if she intended going out that evening. She replied that she could do so if she chose, whereupon Elmer shot her three times, causing her instant death. He had not been paying her attention, and no cause is known for his act. He was at once locked up. A crowd gathered and tried to storm the jail, but its ringleaders were arrested before anything was done. The body of the murdered girl has lain in state in the court-room to-day, and has been viewed by thousands. Her Bohemian countrymen vow vengeance, and in anticipation of an attempted lynching tonight, a strong guard has been posted around the jail.

SHOCKING TRAGEDY.
A Man at Wahpeton, Dakota, Kills a Young Lady, and is Summarily Lynched.
A Man at Wahpeton, Dakota, Kills a Young Lady, and is Summarily Lynched.

Miss Mollie Korbell, of Wahpeton, Dakota, was murdered by deputy sheriff S. S. Elmer. The victim was a respected domestic in Sheriff Miller's family and was entrusted with the management of the household during the family's temporary absence, and at the time of the murder had just given the prisoners in the jail their supper. Elmer and other employees of the sheriff boarded with him, and after supper Elmer asked the deceased if she intended going out. She replied that if she felt like it, she would do so. At this Elmer pulled his revolver and shot her three times—in the arm, below the ear and in the neck. The murderer immediately gave himself up to another deputy sheriff, who locked him in a cell. A great crowd soon gathered and began to prepare ropes and to break into the jail. The police were active, and under direction of the mayor several men were arrested and locked up. The latter belonged to the fire department, and some firemen rang the fire bell. Almost every member of the department gathered, and the mob made a rush for the city hall to tear it down.

A masked mob of 100 determined men then overpowered Sheriff Miller and Deputy Bronte through the cages and took the murderer out. The mob was well organized and headed by resolute men of Whapeton and Breckenridge. The sheriff offered all the physical resistance his 260 pound afforded, but did not attempt to shoot or fight because the mob were all his friends and said the life of the murderer not worth the life of a friend. After the hanging the mob quietly dispersed, and the hundreds of men and women who witnessed the hanging went home satisfied. Elmer said he did not know why he killed the girl, and was sorry that he had done so. When asked if wished to prey he said, "No."

Miss Korbel was twenty-one years old and was highly respected by all who knew her. Elmer had never kept company with her, and had no claim to her attention, and why he should murder the girl is a mystery.
The murderer came from Massachusetts to Minnesota in 1862 and enlisted at Fort Snelling. He has been about Wahpeton two years and has borne a good character, though frequently exhibiting a weakness for strong drink; but he was sober when the murder was committed. He formerly lived in Fargo and is well known throughout the county. Six years ago he was employed by John Haggart, sheriff of Cass county, and served as deputy sheriff. Previous to his arrival at Fargo he had been deputy sheriff at Rochester, Minn. He was given to drinking, more or less, and four years ago Mr. Haggart discharged him. He remained a while longer and then went to James B. Powers' Helendale stock farm. From there he went to Wahpeton, and has since acted as deputy under Sheriff Miller.

ANOTHER ACCOUNT.

The Bohemian farmers began to gather in town towards night. After some consultation it was decided to use strategy, and the Bohemians withdrew. In the middle of the night a sudden outburst of voices near the jail roused the whole town. All the citizens, and those of Breckenridge as well, repaired to the scene. About the jail was gathered a mob of about seventy-five masked men. They made a rush for the jail, but at the command of Sheriff Miller they halted. It was only for a moment, however. They surrounded the sheriff and his twelve deputies, and firmly, though without harsh treatment, hustled them to one side. With crowbars and sledge hammers they then attacked the cell of the prisoner. The wonderful nerve of the murderer was admired even by the most desperate of his lynchers. Elmer sat on his cot in his cell and watched the progress made by the workers who were battering down the cell doors, as if he doubted their skill in such work. Not a word escaped his lips, but when the third steel door that separated him from the mob fell he stood up and presented his head for the noose to be slipped over. When the mob left the jail, Elmer clasped the rope with both hands to keep from being jerked down and appeared perfectly cool. After leaving the court yard, the mob quickened its pace and was soon in a swift race for the bridge. The immense crowd pressed closely about the running prisoner when one partially tripped him and Elmer said: "Don't do that boys, I've got the worst of the deal now." When the mob stepped on the bridge and the rope had been thrown over a stringer, Elmer was asked if he had anything to say. "No, I guess not," he replied. "Why did you kill the girl?" was asked. "I did it in the heat of passion," he said. Elmer was asked if he wanted to send any word to relatives, or if he wished to pray. He said not, and asked the mob if they wanted to tie his hands in front or behind his back. They were tied behind his back. "Are you ready," was asked. "Yes," said Elmer "hoist away." The horrid deed was done; blood atoned for blood. The body was cut down at 4 o'clock by the coroner. The parents of the murdered girl watched every movement of the lynchers with delight.
