Lynching Report Denied.
St. Louis, July 24.—A very brief special to the Post-Dispatch says that one of the negro county officials of Crittenden county, Ark., was hanged by a mob at Marion last night, and that the race war has broken out afresh, and that a terrible state of affairs prevailed.

Memphis, July 24.—The report of a lynching at Marion, Ark., last night and further race troubles in Crittenden county is unfounded.

THE REPORT CONFIRMED.

St. Louis, July 24.—A special from Springfield, Mo., says: Traveling Auditor Townsend, of the Gulf road, arrived in that city at noon from the south, and verifies the report of one of the negro county officials having been lynched by a mob of white men. Townsend says it is a difficult matter to get any details of the proceedings at Marion, which is under the guard of armed men. A general state of excitement prevails. Neither couriers nor messengers are allowed to go in or out and the telegraph operator is confined to the sending of train orders. Townsend states that the victim was a county official and one of the banished eighteen. The mob seized him while he was endeavoring to effect an entrance to the Court House, dragged him to the woods at the edge of the town, and, after a desperate struggle, strung him up. It is claimed that Governor Hughes, at Little Rock, has been called upon for protection, and if this be true, details must be forthcoming. It is also claimed that an armed force of white men have gone from Walnut Ridge to Marion to aid the whites, who look for a serious uprising of the negroes.
marion-marion-1888-07-23.A6:
How long, O Lord, how long will the wild-eyed, long-haired idiotic romancer about Crittenden county be allowed to roam over the face of the earth!

The following harrowing details of a lynching over there, that may be properly classed with "The Letter That Never Came," were telegraphed to THE APPEAL by the Associated Press last night:

IT WAS AWFUL!

St. Louis, Mo., July 24.—A dispatch from Springfield, Mo., says: Traveling Auditor Townsend, of the Gulf road, arrived in that city at noon from the south and verifies the report of one of the negro county officials having been lynched by a mob of white men. Mr. Townsend says that it is a difficult matter to get any details of proceedings at Marion, which is under a guard of armed men, and a great state of excitement prevailing. Neither couriers or messengers are allowed in or out, and the telegraph operator is confined to the sending of train orders. Mr. Townsend states that the victim was a county official and one of the banished eighteen. The mob seized him while he was endeavoring to effect an entrance into the court-house, dragged him to the woods at the edge of the town, and after a desperate struggle strung him up. It is claimed that Gov. Hughes, at Little Rock, has been called upon for protection, and if this be true the details must be forthcoming. It is also claimed that an armed force of white men have gone from Walnut Ridge to Marion to aid the whites who look for a serious uprising of the negroes.

THE WORST KIND OF BOSH.

The rumor of an affair similar to that described by Mr. Eli Perkins Townsend to a Springfield, Mo., reporter stalked through this city all day yesterday. It also made a gallant charge upon St. Louis, as evidenced by numerous inquiries for particulars. The APPEAL yesterday printed a faithful resume of the situation from the beginning up to the time the reporter left Marion Monday afternoon. There was no trouble over there then, or anticipation of any. All that the white and ninety-nine one-hundredths of the colored people there desire is for the banished negroes, who would kill any territory they infest, even were there no other inhabitants, to keep away. It may be a bold assertion, but THE APPEAL does not believe $5,000 would induce any one of them to return. They know what sort of treatment would be meted out to them.

Even Little Rock caught the excitement, as will be seen from the following special telegram to THE APPEAL:

IT IS AWFULLY UNKIND.

LITTLE ROCK, Ark., July 24.—Considerable excitement was caused here today on the circulation of a rumor that the Crittenden county troubles have broken out afresh, and that the whites had last night lynched County Judge Lewis, a colored man. Judge J. W. Blackwood is said to have received a dispatch containing the intelligence this morning. Gov. Hughes has had nothing in confirmation of the news, and if it is true, Crittenden county officials feel able to cope with the existing state of affairs. The Governor says, however, he is ready to act instantly on being called on for assistance, as the laws of Arkansas are supreme and must be obeyed. There is no equivocation in this. Sheriff Werner, of Crittenden, arrived in the city today bringing a couple of prisoners to the penitentiary, but says he knows nothing of the reports. Everything was quiet on his leaving Marion yesterday morning. THE APPEAL correspondent mentioned the affair to Judge John McClure, of this city, who he found at the Capitol tonight.

"I only know what Blackwood's dispatch is said to contain," remarked this biggest of Arkansas Republicans. Everybody knows Judge McClure in this section, as well as a great many outside of this State have the honor of his acquaintance. Powell Clayton, McClure & Co. are the Republican party of this State. "Yes, that is all I know about the matter. They ought to have hung Lewis. He was a bad character. At the Republican State convention in this city, some time ago, Lewis objected to something that I said, and I told him then he would not last until the election, nor he hasn't. He evidently didn't know the whites of Crittenden county as well as I do. They treated Lewis very nicely. Bought him a ticket, took him to the train and put him aboard, told him to leave the country and not come back again. Lewis did not leave, but came here and stayed a few days, when he made fool of himself. He thought the whites down there didn't mean anything when they told him to leave the county. But they did, and he found out what they meant, too, and I don't blame them one bit. He deserved to be hung, and so does any other man who thinks he is bigger than the law."

Astwood, United States Consul at San Domingo, recently addressed a communication to General Figuero, San Dominican Minister of Interior, containing a proposition for the privilege of exhibiting the remains of the immortal Christopher Columbus in the United States. It is more than probable that Astwood and the American will carry to their dying bed the just, fitting and eloquent rebuke given the former in answer to his communication containing the shameful proposition. Ministers Thompson and Astwood do not seem to be reflecting a great deal of credit upon the present Democratic administration, these days.

THE "WHITE CAPS" are causing the white people of some parts of Southern Indiana and Illinois about as much trouble as the "Ku-Klux" did our people in some parts of the South. The former are but an outgrowth of the latter, and if they do nothing else will perhaps teach some parts of the country the fallacy of allowing organized bodies or single persons to transgress the law with impunity. Some day when white county officials of an opposite political faith, or who are displeasing to a set, organization or mob, are taken out and hung, the people of this country will wake up to the fact that such successful mobs as the "Ku-Klux Klans," "White Caps" and Marion County, Ark., crowd that without cause hung one of its colored county officers, set precedents that are bound to react and in so doing strike home, reaching those who ignore such things as long as the poor and defenseless Negro alone is affected.

THE SOUTH is helping on a few bla-lant demagogues who can be made very useful. It helps put them in office and cries, "see what we are doing for the colored man." It joins hands with the Negro on Prohibition, and it has junkets in the dark with him on the labor questions, but while it s patting him on the back and say-ing "talk it brother (for us)" it all the time keeps an iron hand upon him in some form so that the solid South shall not be attacked and that our equal rights may be kept in the background. It joins hands with an individual but not with a race. The one is used for mere personal interest, and vanity and love of gain, popularity and the position of so-called leader, while the many sit in the same old darkness where the South intends they shall sit so long as it can manipulate the few. Rise up, Northern colored men—not merely Northern colored politicians, though we do appeal to their honor in this, but the Northern colored people—and help emancipate these brothers in the South, who are unable, by force of sad circumstances to strike for themselves effectually. Rise up and vote for the Republican party, whose platform helps the most to this end. Each one can thus be a Moses.

THE DISPATCHES the past week tell us of another dastardly outrage that should cause a blush of shame to rise to the cheeks of every resident of this country with its farce of a government. At a recent election in Marion County, Ark., several colored officials were elected. For some reason or other (more than likely the old cause of so much trouble in the South, prejudice, the whites determined to get rid of these colored officers, and ordered them to leave that part of the country. It seems that they did leave, but the past week one returned and was taken out by a mob of white brutes, worse than murderers, and hanged. Being in the minority and fearing just treatment at the hands of the enraged colored residents, they sought and received aid from the whites in that vicinity and also called upon the Governor for "protection." Should the colored people of Marion rise up and sweep that locality clean of such infernal brutes, they would simply be doing themselves justice and the whole country an infinite amount of good. Will our people in Southern localities where they are numerically the strongest, ever learn to provide and prepare themselves to strike back when outraged and hounded, as many members of the race are every week? How long, OH! HOW LONG is this sort of thing to continue? It seems that Providence, as well as the Government,has forsaken our people in many parts of the South.

THE RACE WAR,
Which Has Been Agitating an Arkansas County.
The Return of One of the Refugees Renews the Excitement-A Colored Leader Talks.
MARION, Ark., July 22.—[Special.]—The Crittenden county trouble took on a new phase today. When the noon train arrived from Memphis Dr. N. J. Stith stepped off. Stith is one of the colored men who was put in a wagon and carted to the Mississippi by a detachment of white men carrying Winchesters, directed to go on board a boat, and never return to the county again.

Stith's return was a great surprise. It was not expected that any of the banished would be seen here again. While little was said about the penalty of coming back, there was a clear understanding what it would be to many. Therefore Stith's appearance this noon, looked like doing the worse. A letter was received here this morning by the mother-in-law of D. W. Lewis, the banished county judge, saying that he would be in today. No confidence was put in it, but at the same time provision was made to meet the unexpected emergency.

There were men at the depot when the train arrived to take care of Lewis if he came. He did not come, but Stith got off. Deputy Constable Tom Adams, a colored man, immediately stepped forward, told Stith he was a prisoner, took him to the county jail and locked him up. Adams stated later that he did not know the charge against Stith, but had arrested him under order. He immediately made a trip to Sheriff Werner, who lives several miles from Marion, and reported the arrest. Stith had not been here an hour before he realized.

WHAT A RISK HE HAD TAKEN

in coming back in face of the notice given him by the white men's organization. He had been writing to parties here, among them County Treasurer Ferguson, begging the privilege of returning long enough to settle his business. But he had come without waiting for the answer. His explanation was that his nephew, who lived in his house here, had written him that Mrs. Stith was sick, and that it would be all right to come and see her.

Presuming that the boy had authority from the white men for what he wrote, Stith says he got on the train and came without any suspicion of danger.

He refers to County Judge Lewis, County Clerk Ferguson, Editor Fleming and the others as the "ring," and says that since the banishment he had kept aloof from them in Memphis. This letter was produced after Stith's arrest today, and it was a big point in his favor. His previous character was also taken into consideration.

It was well for Lewis that he did not come, for there would have been little hesitation in his case. Stith spent the afternoon in jail, not knowing what was to become of him. While the leading white citizens were considering the situation, Stith's wife, for whose sake he had taken the dangerous step, sat in the door of the jail crying. They were but recently married in Nashville. She is a teacher in one of the Crittenden county schools. Some of the younger white men were for taking prompt action in Stith's case. There were those in favor of hanging him. The older men protested against this, and insisted that the law be allowed to take its course. An explanation of the grounds on which Stith had been arrested helped to allay the sentiment that favored lynching. The papers in his case showed that one of the indictments returned last night was against him. He is charged with being one of those

WHO CONSPIRED AGAINST THE WHITE PEOPLE and with implication in the sending of the anonymous notes to white citizens to leave the county within five days. Stith insists that he had cut loose entirely from the others, but it is claimed that there was evidence before the grand jury to convict him with them. The evidence was given by colored men who, it is said, admitted with great reluctance the existence of the conspiracy, and gave names and plan.

WILL STAY IN JAIL.

Court adjourned yesterday for the semi-annual term, and will not meet again until January. As there is a decided indisposition to give bail for Stith he will likely remain in custody six months. The arrest of Stith had the affect to arouse the white people. The excitement was dying out. Pickets and patrols had been discontinued, but now the feeling is intense again.

AN APPEAL FOR PEACE.

At the Pleasant Grove Baptist church, the largest colored church in Arkansas, Elder Robinson had a large congregation. He made his entire discourse and appealed to his people to keep at peace with the white folks. "Go home and be at peace," he said. "I told you last Sunday let us go home and be quiet. I told you there was no race war in Crittenden county. A few men can't make a race war. They tell me you people all got excited. Some left the fields and their work. I have never heard of anybody trying to deprive you of life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness. There has not been a white man to come here to interfere with you, has there? (Cries of no, no.) You have met here at all hours and had your meetings and gone home without being molested, haven't you? (Cries of yes, bress de Lawd.) I tell you the only imposement I ever had in this place was from my own race. Somebody is trying to get up excitement, and if they do they will be the first to run."

A Reign of Terror.

St. Louis, July 24.—The Crittenden race war has broken out again. A special to the Post-Dispatch says that one of the negro county officials was lynched by a mob at Marion last night. A terrible state of affairs prevails.

The victim was one of the county officers and one of the banished eighteen. The mob seized him while he was endeavoring to gain entrance to the court house, dragged him to the woods and after a desperate struggle, strung him up.

Sheriff Werner Has No Writs to Serve on the Caucasians of Crittenden.
Sheriff Werner, of Crittenden county, Ark., was in Memphis yesterday. An APPEAL reporter meeting that official, desired to know what progress had been made in arresting the parties indicted for complicity in the recent troubles in that neck of the woods.

"None at all, further than the arrest and release on good bond of Dr. Stith."

"Were not some of the white men indicted residents of Marion, and have they not been there all the time?"

"Who said there were any white men indicted?"

"No one, positively, but that is the general impression. Were there any?"

"That I cannot tell, because no arrests have been made."

BUILDOZING IN ARKANSAS.
Preparing for a "Democratic Victory" in
Crittenden County.
There arrived in the city yesterday.
Preparing for a "Democratic Victory" in Crittenden County.

There arrived in the city yesterday morning two very intelligent colored men, J. W. Ramsey and York Byers, who were among those who were driven out of Crittenden county, Ark., a few weeks ago, by the white regulators. Ramsey was a Deputy Sheriff, and with the remaining colored county officials were shipped to Memphis, where they scattered, some going to St. Louis, others to places in Kentucky and these gentlemen to this city, where they hope to find employment. The story of their expulsion from Crittenden county was most graphically related to a Commercial Gazette reporter by Ramsey yesterday afternoon, and was about as follows:

"It was on the morning of July 12th last, when some three hundred white men, all armed, surrounded and entered the Court-house at Marion, Crittenden county, a part of them coming into Clerk Dan Ferguson's office, in which I was a deputy. Ferguson was a colored man, and there were two deputies besides myself, all colored. A country physician named Bingham acted as the spokesman for the visitors, and called the depties out one by one, and said: 'Gentlemen, this county is too small for you and for us. One must leave. We have decided it shall be you, and if you do not go we hope you'll get to heaven.' During all this they had their guns cocked, and the leader held in his hand a resignation for County Clerk Ferguson to copy and sign. This he was compelled to do under penalty of death. Then, without giving us an opportunity of even putting on our coats, they took us back of the Court-house, searched us and placed us under guard—four to each man—armed with Winchesters. The town was then scoured, and Dr. Steth, Henry, Belby, Fleckehn, doctor and teachers, were taken out and subjected to the same treatment we had undergone. A Masonic Lodge, a band and a children's gathering were broken up by these marauders. Finally we were put in the road and marched two and two through the town. When a mile outside we were overtaken by a wagon prepared for the journey, loaded in and carried to Mound City, six miles distant, under guard of horsemen, all armed. At Mound City we were supplied with steamboat tickets for Memphis, a guard accompanying us to that point, and upon taking leave of us the spokesman said: 'We have no apologies to make for what we have done to-day. All we can say is just this: If any of you ever return your lives shall pay the penalty.' So we were landed at Memphis."

Barbarous Treatment of a Chinaman by His Countrymen.

MARYSVILLE, August 1st.—The Chinese garden across the Yuba river, a few miles north of Marysville, has been the scene of shockingly barbarous treatment of a Chinaman by some of his own countrymen, within the past week. The victim was found by a white man suspended in a shed by a rope passed under his shoulders. He said he had been kept in that position three days without food or water.

The Chinese were told that they must bring their captive to town and deliver him to the authorities. They lowered him to the ground and promised to bring him in, but nothing has since been seen of him.

Investigation is being made by the officers of the law. The victim was employed as a domestic on a ranch in the neighborhood. The Chinese captors are known to have threatened to kill anybody caught stealing from them.

PORT TOWNSEND. Dec. 4.—The stevedor.
PORT TOWNSEND, Dec. A. The stevedoring and ship-brokerage firm of R. W. De Lion & Co. disposed of their business yesterday to the Puget Sound Stevedoring Company of which Mr. J. P. Betts is resident manager. Mr. De Lion has formed a co-partnership with Mr. Joseph C. Barstow for the purpose of dealing in doors, saashes, paints, oils and general house-furnishing supplies. These gentlemen have leased the large building recently erected on Water street by Judge Kuhn, and will be ready for business about the first of January. Mr. De Lion will be yesterday for California to purchase stock.

Much complaint is heard among the stable-keepers and draymen concerning the extreme scarcity of hay. Farmers in the surrounding country have refused to bale their hay this year, intending to wait until the spring for higher prices.

A few days since an Indian woman was discovered on the beach near Port Discovery in almost a dying condition. She was conveyed to the hospital for the county poor, and, upon examination, she was found to be suffering from severe burns all over her body has since been learned that during some time the probably rheumatism, her relatives had attempted, after their usual custom, to cure her by the use of fire or heated irons, and during the course of the horrible torture the woman's reason was totally destroyed. As soon as the burns have healed an examination will be made by Probate Judge Whittlesey as to the advisability of sending her to the asylum.

H. F. Beecher, who was expected to be here this week, will not arrive for about two weeks. Much disappointment is felt because the Knights, of Yellias, of which order Beecher is the instituting officer of this district, as they will not now be able to institute the uniform rank, lately organized here, previous to their grand anniversary ball, which takes place next Friday evening.

Burned at the Stake.

Seattle, W. T., special: A "Post-Intelligencer" special from Port Townsend gives an account of the burning of an India woman at the stake near Port Ludlow, yesterday. She was brought to Port Townsend this morning and taken to the poorhouse. She is terribly burned from the feet to the neck. The man who brought her in found her on the beach near Ludlow, almost unconscious. She told him in broken Chinook that male and female members of her tribe had tied her to a stake, piled brushwood around her and set fire to it and left her to perish. By herculean efforts she freed herself. The alleged reason for the act was that she had contracted an odious disease. The woman is 19 years old.

Shot and Killed by His Nephew. GADSDEN, Ala., Dec. 24.—Jesse J. Taylor, an old and highly respected citizen of this county, was to-day shot and instantly killed by his nephew, Arch Craze, about 25 years old. Taylor was trying to prevent a difficulty between Craze and a man named Lancaster, when the former turned, and, placing a pistol against Taylor's head, shot him dead. Craze escaped, but a Sheriff's posse is in pursuit. At Hafflin, Ala., last night, Turner Bryant was shot and killed by his father-in-law, R. T. Chambers. Bryant's wife had left him and was living with her father. He went to the house and forced his way in, and was killed. Chambers surrendered. A Negro Opens Fire on Regulators.
CHARLOTTE, N. C., Dec. 24.—Sam Harting, a negro, living in York county, on the South Carolina line, had a white woman living with him whom he alleged to be his lawful wife. Harting of late had become so defiant that the white women feared him, and last night a crowd of "Regulators" visited him to warn him that he must leave the county in a given number of hours. When the Regulators informed the negro of their mission he swore that he would not leave at their command. He drew a large pistol and opened fire upon the men, killing one instantly and wounding others. He then made his escape to the woods. Men are on hunt for him, and if caught he will be lynched.

Called Out of His House and Shot.

HUNTINGSBURG, Ind., Dec. 24.—Sebastian Hobbs, a farmer living three miles south of Bird's Eyes, Dubous county, was called out of his house on Saturday night and two shots were fired at him. One shot struck him in the abdomen and killed him. A man named Smith was arrested on suspicion. Hobbs has made himself obnoxious to the White Caps by procuring evidence against them and urging prosecution. He had a wire stretched around his yard as protection against the White Caps.

A Woman and Her Grandson Burned to Death.

SCRANTON, Dec. 24.—Early this morning a fire occurred at Forest City, in Susquehanna county, which destroyed the home of Mrs. John Priestly. The woman and her grandson were caught in the flames and burned to death. The woman received $3,000 four months ago on the death of her husband, and by some the fire is regarded as being the means of covering up a darker crime, as she is believed to have kept large sums of money in the house.

A Steamer Burned and Seven Lives Lost.

SEATTLE, W. T., Dec. 24.—The steamer Lief Erickson, burned at Alki, a point five miles west of this city, at 5 o'clock this afternoon. She is a total loss. Seven lives were lost. Miss Annie A. Tollner of Sidney, Mason county; J. H. Noreus, manager of Noreus Brick Yard Company, Sidney; Jack Simmons, half-breed fisherman; T. Smith of Smith, Taylor & Co., Colby; unknown man and wife, and unknown woman.

The "Q." Dynamiter Found Guilty.

GENEVA, Ill., Dec. 24.—In the case of Bauereisen, chief of the dynamiters at Aurora, who has been on trial here for several days past, the jury returned a verdict of guilty and fixed his sentence at two years. The crime of which he was accused was conspiracy to injure the property of the Chicago. Burlington and Quincy Railroad Company with dynamite. Bauereisen was one of the striking engineers of that road.

HOMICIDE.
On Sunday night last Dave Witherspoon, colored, shot and killed a white man named William J. Harten. Monday morning Dave came to town and reported the occurrence to Trial Justice Bell. His story is to the effect that on Sunday night Harten and another man came to his house, 3½ miles from town, on the Pinckney road, acting in a boisterous manner, firing guns or pistols into the house, knocking down the doors and smashing the windows. After warning them to desist and without effect, he fired upon his assailants, killing Harten. Trial Justice Bell referred Dave to the coroner.

Coroner Caldwell was notified of the occurrence and he proceeded at once to hold an inquest. The following jury was impanneled: R. E. Gettys, Foreman; E. L. Owens, J. T. Latham, E. R. Stuart, James E. Gettys, R. S. Moore, Charles H. Sandifer, J. D. Sherer, W. E. Sutton, W. L. Thomas, George Bird, colored, R. S. Nance, colored, Henry Torbet, J. C. Carson.

Dr. R. Andral Bratton was summoned as a medical expert, and furnished the following written statement:

"This is to certify that I have performed a post-mortem examination on the body of William J. Harten, deceased, and found a gunshot wound, entering the brain through the left orbit, causing his death."

Mr. C. H. Sandifer, Lydia Witherspoon, Ann Witherspoon, Mr. Wm. Bradford and Dave Witherspoon were examined as witnesses.

Mr. Sandifer's testimony was to the effect that at about 2 o'clock Monday morning, Dave Witherspoon came to his house with an evasive story about two men having come to his house Sunday night, and that one was there yet and that something must be the matter with him; that he thought one had shot the other. Witness and Ed. Estis went to Dave's house with him and found Harten dead. In the words of the witness: "I told Dave the shooting must have been done with a gun; and if you shot, you tell the straight tale. He said he shot once, out of the window, and I told him that was the shot that hit. I started home, and he begged me to stay, as he said he was afraid others would come back."

The testimony of Lydia and Ann Witherspoon is to the effect that Harten is the father of Lydia's two children and that

came there for the purpose of taking the children away, such being the threats of Harten and a man accompanying him whom they did not know Admittance into the house being refued them, they commenced firing upon it and making threats. Both testified that Dave fired his gun at the intruders.

Mr. Bradford testified tha Harten was at his house twice Sunday night, the last time at about 9 o'clock, when he wanted some of witness' sons to go with him, but they refused.

Dave Witherspoon's testimony was as follows:

When I shot, I did not see any one through the window. I shot just to scare them away. I did not know who was around the house. At first, they came on their horses and said there were two children there belonging to some white man, and the Regulators had said they must be given up before midnight. I told him to go away, that all the white people in the neighborhood knew me, and that no one but a mean man would bother me. They rode off and came back walking. Mr. Harten yelled out, "Form yourselves, boys; form yourselves; fire!" Two shots were fired into the kitchen where my wife and her two children were sitting. I ran into another room, begging them all the time to go away. I told him I knew him. He did go for a while. After a while he came on the piazza and struck the door. I begged him to go away. He went around to the side of the house. I heard him say: "We will put the dynamites under the house and blow them up." About that time he threw a big rock into the window, and then came around to the fire place and shot through another window twice. I told him I must do something if he did not leave. I reached around the door, Lydia holding to me, and fired. I did not take any aim, and did not see any one. Did not know if I had hit or killed any one. Did not hear any noise.

The jury rendered the following verdict: "That the said William J. Harten came to his death by or from a gun shot wound in the left eye, by Dave Witherspoon, colored, from the inside of his house, and we believe, in self-defense."

On the coroner's warrant, Dave was lodged in jail on Monday evening.

Harten was 25 or 30 years old and unmarried. Lying near his dead body was a "bull dog" pistol of 38 calibre, every chamber of which was loaded. Examination showed that two sizes of balls were fired into the house, on 32 and the other 38 calibre. Lydia Witherspoon, mother of the two children of whom Harten is the reputed father, is the wife of Dave Witherspoon, the homicide.

OFFICIAL BONDS.

The board of county commissioners met in their office last Thursday and approved the bonds of E. A. Crawford for Sheriff, and S. L. Purseley for Coroner.

Sheriff Crawford's bond is in the sum of $10,000 with the following sureties: E. A. Crawford, Jr., James P. Crawford, J. A. Erwin, J. S. Bratton, Jr., R. Mendenhall, A. E. McFadden, J. M. McFadden.

Coroner Purseley's bond is in the sum of $2,000 with the following sureties: William McGill, James L. McGill.

The bonds of the Treasurer and Auditor have not yet been submitted, as these are appointive offices.

Probate Judge McCorkle took charge of his office yesterday. None of the other officers elect will enter upon their duties until about the first of the year, this arrangement being their preference, though the old officers are ready to vacate at any time.

The long and faithful service of two of these officers requires more than a passing notice. Jes. F. Wallace was elected Clerk of the Court in January, 1866, and entered upon his duties on the 15th of February of that year. R. H. Glenn was elected Sheriff in November, 1866, and entered upon his duties on the 20th of December. Both these officials have been in constant service since their first election twenty-one years ago, and while their period of service is almost without precedent in the history of the county, thus marking their popularity, it can be truthfully said that the positions have never been filled in York county by more competent, efficient or faithful officers, and they retire with the plaudits of their county men, well done ye good and faithful servants.

Another Slaughter of Colored People a Spanish Camp
Special to the Gazette.
HOUSTON, TEX., March 23 — News has been received in this city of a double killing at Spanish Camp, in Wharton county, the scene of the recent tragedy where six negroes were shot and killed and their house burned over them. No particulars have come to hand further than two more colored men have gone the way of their brethren who were murdered last month. Since the murder of six negroes the Governor was called upon to send Rangers into the county to aid the authorities in maintaining peace. These aids to the county officers have been in the neighborhood for some days. It appears their presence has not had a soothing effect upon the people, many of whom it is stated, are leaving upon the receipt of an invitation to quit the country. Although the foregoing facts come from a reliable source they are discredited in this city.

Two Negroes Killed.
CHICAGO, Mar. 24.—A dispatch from Richmond, Texas., says: A courier just arrived from Wharton states that two negroes were murdered on Tuesday night in Wharton county near the recent scene of the massacre of six negroes at Spanish Camp. This killing was on Battel's plantation. Gov. Ross sent a company of rangers to Wharton county to suppress the lawlessness. James Wygall, of Clarke plantation, also living near Spanish Camp, came here yesterday armed with a rifle, stating he left on account of a threatening letter warning him to leave the county. Gov. Ross says he will send in the whole military of the State if necessary, to suppress the lawless element.

A Young War.

RICHMOND, Tex., March 26.—Two more colored men were killed near Spanish Camp, the scene of the recent butchery of six colored men and women. The Thursday night murders occurred on the plantation known as the Battled place. A reign of terror exists in Wharton county among the colored population. It is believed some secret society has been organized among the white planters for the purpose of expelling and killing obnoxious regressors and their white sympathizers. Among the latter is Henry Wyatt, a well-to-white farmer, who arrived here yesterday from near Spanish Camp. Ross has recently ordered a company of state rangers to report to the sheriff at Wharton for the purpose of keeping the peace and preventing bloodshed during the coming session of the district court, when it is expected a militant of assassins will be denounced before the grand jury. The presence of rangers, however, does not prevent parties whose lives are threatened, like Wyatt, from leaving the county, as they have no faith in the ability of rangers to prevent their assassination. The condition of affairs is nearly as bad as it was in Kemper county, Mississippi, twelve years ago.

South and West.
JAMES W. TATE, the absconding treasurer of Kentucky, whose defalcation is now placed at $250,000, has been seen in Canada. The Legislature has decided to impeach him.

BALLARD BRONSTON, son of a prominent official, has killed the Sheriff of Madison County, Ky.

THREE American prospectors were killed by Indians at Priest Lake, Washington Territory.

MRS. JOSEPH PARKER, an insane woman of Stewartstown, W. Va., saturated her clothing with coal oil and set herself on fire. Before her husband could come to the rescue she met a terrible death.

THOMAS BROWN, one of the men employed to fill the places of the striking Burlington engineers, was killed by unknown parties at St. Joseph, Mo.

All the switchmen and brakemen employed by the Chicago, Burlington & Quincy Railroad have struck in aid of the engineers.

At Spanish Camp, Texas, the scene of the recent killing of six colored men, armed whites have again murdered two negroes, and Governor Ross has sent a troop of rangers there to suppress further outbreaks.

THE Georgia State Republican Convention has met at Saundersville and elected delegates to the National Convention, who are pledged to support Senator Sherman for the Presidential nomination.

GOVERNOR ROSS, of Texas, has promulgated a call for an extra session of the Legislature. This is made necessary to consider the surplus in the State Treasury, which now amounts to over $10,000,000.

from the committee on platform and resolutions
We, your committee on platform and resolutions, beg leave to submit the following resolutions, and recommend the adoption thereof:

1. The Republicans of Texas, in state convention assembled, renew their allegiance to the principles of the Republican party upon which they have achieved so many glorious victories.

2. We ratify and confirm the principles of our national platform of 1884.

3. We condemn the free trade doctrine and sentiments expressed in the message of President Cleveland to Congress.

4. We favor a tariff for protection in order to afford security to our industries and protection to the rights and wages of the laborer and mechanic.

5. We recognize the importance of sheep husbandry in this state and the danger threatening its future prospects, and we, therefore, respect the demands of this important agricultural interest for a full and adequate protection of this product.

6. We demand that our general government at Washington make ample provisions for the construction of a first-class deep water harbor on our gulf coast, at such a point as may be designated by the government engineers, and that Congress concentrate all appropriations of money for that purpose.

7. We demand in the event Congress should fail in the early establishment of a deep water harbor, that the Legislature of Texas shall make sufficient and liberal appropriations to commence this work in order to prove to the country at large the good faith and the earnestness of the citizens of Texas.

8. We lament the death of Roscoe Conkling. The Republic is bereft by his death of one of her noblest sons and humanity one of its grandest and most chivalrous champions and one of the brightest intellects that ever adorned the pages of our country's history.

9. We recommend to the convention the adoption of the following resolutions:

Resolved, that our Texas delegation to the national Republican convention at Chicago, be not instructed as to choice of candidate for President and Vice-president, in order that they may be governed in their action by the judgment and advice of the delegations from the doubtful northern states, that in case victory is to be with us, must necessarily furnish the votes to elect.

Resolved by the Republicans in convention assembled, that they regard the efforts of a small number of people of Texas in establishing and supporting a "Home" for the maimed and diseased ex-Confederate soldiers as praiseworthy, but unwise.

Resolved, that we believe it to be the duty, and it should be the pride of the state, to endow, or keep up by appropriations, a "Home" for the helpless ex-Union and Confederate soldiers and sailors, so as to prevent their becoming a burden upon the charity of communities.

Resolved, that a copy of these resolutions be forwarded to His Excellency, L. S. Ross, governor, requesting that he submit them to the Senate and House of Representatives of the state of Texas.

Respectfully submitted,

A. J. Rosenthal,
Chairman Committee on Platform and Resolutions.

J. C. Bigcer, Secretary Committee.
J. C. BIGGER, Secretary Committee.

Rangers sent to Hempstead—A Charter Filed—Reward Offered.

Special to the Gazette.

AUSTIN, TEX., May 23.—Adjutant-General King to-day issued orders to Captain McMurray with a detachment of rangers to report at Hempstead, in consequence of excitement from the assassination Saturday last of Steven Alchin by Deputy Sheriff Dick Springfield and a farmer named Jack McDade. Adjutant-General King has ordered the detachment of rangers hitherto doing duty in Wharton county there, making in all about ten men. Among the instructions to the rangers is to see that the good citizens of the town and county are protected and especially that there shall be no intimidation of witnesses at the trial of the assassins which comes off Monday. It is understood that Adjutant King during a visit to Hempstead Tuesday morning found McDade and the prisoners, Springfield and Jack McDade, barricated in the court house; that General King sent word to McDade to come and see him; that McDade refused, that Adjutant King sent McDade word the prisoners must be put in jail either at Hempstead or somewhere else; that the courthouse was no place to hold the prisoners and should be free of access to all citizens; that if he did not vacate it with the prisoners he (McDade) would be put out by force. The position of the rangers will be that of a force to preserve peace and prevent intimidation of witnesses. In other words, they have orders to break the reign of terror and uphold the supremacy of law. Adjutant General King says he had interviews with leading citizens of Hempstead, and there was evidently no intention of resorting to lynch law. Their aim seemed to be to remove all that obstructs the law.

The following charter was filed yesterday: The Clayton Co-operative Machine Company of Grayson county, for the encouragement of agriculture and the procuring farm machinery; capital, $50,000; incorporators—M. D. L. Bax, J. J. Johnson, C. B. Polk, C. C. Bomberger and J. W. Pitt.

Governor Ross has offered a reward of $250 for the arrest of Albert Whitter, who committed a murder in Madison county some time ago.
stephen-alchin-hampstead-1888-05-26.A8:
TROUBLE AT HEMPSTEAD.
A Tragedy That Grew Out of a Newspaper Article!
state of affairs exists at Hempstead, a town twenty miles south of this city, and the county seat of Waller county. About three months ago an article appeared in the Hempstead Guard, a weekly newspaper, severely criticizing the action of certain county officers, among them the sheriff. Deputy Sheriff Chambers, accompanied by a friend, demanded of the editor the name of the author. He was informed that a man named Allchin was responsible for its appearance. Chambers and his friend met Allchin on the street and a pistol fight ensued, in which Chambers was killed and his friend and Allchin both severely wounded. Some weeks after these parties made friends and it was supposed the matter had been finally settled, but such was not the case.

Last Saturday, while Allchin was driving his buggy, he was fired on by another deputy sheriff, the ball entering the back of the head, causing instant death. It is claimed that Allchin had threatened the life of the deputy. Jack McLean, a son of the sheriff, who was present when the shot was fired, was arrested and placed in jail. The news of the assassination rapidly spread over the city and county, and the indignation was so great that the sheriff was compelled to call out a company of military to prevent mob law. The governor was telegraphed for aid, and General King was immediately dispatched to the scene of trouble. He at once ordered another company to reinforce the one on duty, and at present matters stand in statu quo, with an enormous undercurrent, which may belch forth at any moment and cause bloodshed.

In the meantime, several mass meetings have been held by the good citizens of the county and resolutions adopted to the effect that they should never cease their efforts to bring to justice all violators of the law and purge the county of the desperate element. Waller is one of the most productive counties in the state, and possesses a class of industrious and intelligent people.

A Mass Meeting of Citizens Call on Governor Ross for Help.
Special Telegram to the Statesman.

HEMPSTEAD, May 24.—At the mass meeting this afternoon, comprising about 500 citizens of Waller county, the following resolution was passed unanimously:

Resolved, That a committee of two citizens from each justice's precinct in the county be elected by this meeting, whose duty it shall be to prepare a calm, dispassionate and truthful statement of the present deplorable condition of affairs in this county, and submit the same to Gov. L. S. Ross, with an earnest request that he take such action as he legally and constitutionally can, as the chief executive of the state, and as, in his judgment, he may deem proper for the enforcement of the laws and protection of life in this county.

A motion was made and carried that a committee of five be chosen to draw up a petition to Thomas S. McDade, asking him to resign the office of sheriff, and to state why the resignation is requested. The report of the committee being returned to the meeting, 108 of the leading citizens present affixed their names.

A message was received to-day from Adjutant-General King saying a troop of rangers would be sent to quiet the town. The excitement is going down rapidly. Up to a late hour to-night the Johnston Guards have not been relieved. One thing is certain, this reign of terror and the fraticidal strife threatening us, is a disgrace to the people of Texas. There is no excuse for its continuance another hour, when Governor Ross is so well posted concerning the cause and remedy. The people of Waller county would welcome martial law to the present state of affairs.

Special Telegram to the Statesman.
HEMPSTEAD, Tex., May 29.—A preliminary examination of Deputy Sheriff Dick Springfield and Jack McDade, charged with murdering S. W. Allchin, opened today. Many witnesses are present. The state has a short-hand reporter employed. Captain McMurray, with his rangers, have headquarters in the county jail and alone in charge of the prisoners. The rangers guard the stairways and entrance to the court room, searching all on entering. The case will probably take three days to conclude. Judge Burkhart is on hand watching events. He has had no occasion to issue the mandates of the law. All is quiet and a large crowd closely watching the trial. The rangers arrested a pistol-toter this morning and jailed him—the first case of the kind in a long time. They are after more.

The Hempstead Horror.
HEMPSTEAD, June 4.—Justice R. M. Thornton in one minute after District Attorney Hannay had made the closing argument in the case of Springfield and McDade, decided that the case was not bailable and refused the defendants bail. They will be sent to the jail of another county for safe keeping at once. The people here now breathe free and feel that the reign of terror and bloodshed, which has so long disgraced Waller county will be checked and one of the best counties of the state redeemed to civilization. There is no excitement. The rangers are in charge of the prisoners and everything is orderly.

stephen-alchin-hampstead-1888-05-26.A20:
THE BRENHAM ASSASSINATION.
The Allchin murder at Hempstead was a fearful, bloody and cowardly crime. But it was committed in broad open daylight, on the streets of the town, in full view of the public. There was no attempt at concealment. It, therefore, lacked some degree of the horror and all of the bloody mystery which, like the darkness of the night on which it was perpetrated, still surrounds the Brenham assassination. McDade and Springfield, at Hempstead, at least showed themselves to their intended victim. The Brenham assassin, like a prowling hyena, stealthily crept upon Hoffman and Holt. Neither had any suspicion of danger. The fatal buckshot, delivered with an intensity of malignity equal to the profound secrecy with which the murder was planned, were sped by a hand as terribly mysterious as that of the unknown midnight fiend who has slain four women in the same neighborhood in London within a short time past. Is there no way to stop these dreadful crimes which are blackening the name of the civilized world?

He had hardly closed the door as he went outside when the cowardly wretch in concealment turned his gun loose on the unsuspecting victim who fell mortally wounded and very soon afterward died. The assassin must have left the scene of his terrible deed immediately after firing the fatal shot as a number of citizens hastened to Mr. McDade's home upon hearing the report of the gun, but no trace of the assassin could be found.

This morning at 1 o'clock Sheriff George Ellis received a telegram from Deputy Sheriff Thornton of Waller county asking for the loan of blood-bounds to trail the murderer. A reporter called at the county jail this morning and visited Jack McDade, a nephew of the murdered man, who, with Dick Springfield, is under indictment for the killing of Allchin in Hempstead some months ago. Young McDade was a deputy under his uncle towards the close of the latter's administration. To the reporter he intimated his belief that the assassination of his uncle was instigated by thirst vengeance on the part of Allchin's friends. Be this as it may, however, the murder of poor McDade was cowardly, cold-blooded and most dastardly in all its hideous bearings. He was elected as sheriff fourteen years ago and for seven consecutive times the people of Waller county evidenced their confidence in him by re-electing him sheriff. In September last he resigned the position and retired to private life. He was known as a brave and efficient officer and commanded the high respect of his fellow citizens. He was essentially a man of peace and during his official career he seldom went armed. While firm and fearless in the discharge of his duty, he never became involved in difficulties or fueds.

From a passenger who came from Hempstead on the afternoon train it was learned that a young man named James Blossingame had been arrested on suspicion. Blossingame had been living some months at the name of Mr. Allchin whose husband was killed by Jack McDade and Dick Springfield some months ago. A horse was tracked from McDade's residence to the Allchin residence and upon this the young man was arrested.

WALLER COUNTY'S LAST TRAGEDY.

Special to the Gazette

HEMPSTEAD, TEX., Nov. 27.—Joe Blossingame, jr., was arrested here this morning on strong circumstantial evidence for the assassination of ex-Sheriff T. S. McDade last evening. The assassin was mounted on horseback and riding up to the back garden fence dismounted, knocked off two pickets, walked through the garden and concealed himself near the well. Captain McDade went to the well to get water for his son who was sick in bed. As he stepped out a shot was fired, filling him with buckshot. This morning the horse was tracked to where Blossingame lived, three-quarters of a mile from the scene of the tragedy. Also the foot prints were measured and corresponded with the boot worn by the party arrested. A double-barrel shotgun was found in the house with one barrel freshly discharged. The load of the other barrel was drawn and the shot compared exactly with that taken from the body of the decease. Blossing-game's examining trial comes up tomorrow.

KANSAS CITY, Dec. 12.—Word was received here this evening from the village of Westport that the bodies of two men had been found hanging to a tree at a point near a school house, six miles south, or ten miles from Kansas City. The coroner left to-night for the scene of the discovery, but as the roads are bad, it is doubtful whether further advices can be obtained before morning. Federation of Labor.
St. Louis, December 12th.—The American Federation of Labor resumed its session this morning. A special committee, to report on that section of President Gomber's address referring to the eight-hour law, was appointed.

The President suggested the formation of eight-hour clubs in all cities and towns to concentrate the movement, and that on February 22d next mass meetings on the subject be held all over the country.

A Volunteer Naval Militia Urged.
New York, December 12th.—The Board of Trade this afternoon resolved to ask the State Legislature to pass a bill authorizing the enrollment of a volunteer naval militia, to act in conjunction with the land volunteer forces in defense of the coast and harbors. This action was taken after consultation with Secretary Whitney and prominent naval officers.

A resolution was adopted asking Congress to pass the bill now pending in regard to the Nicaragua Canal Company.

A Remarkable Case.
CANAJOHARIE (N. Y.), December 12th.—Miss Flora France, 22 years of age, has for 20 months been unable to retain food, and her body wasted until she weighed only 50 pounds. A few days ago she announced that it had been revealed to her in a vision that she would have no further trouble. She was given supper and ate it with apparent relish, and since that time she has gained gradually until now it is believed she will ultimately recover.

An Express Messenger's Steal.
Waco (Tex.), December 12th.—H. T. Hawe, an employee of the Pacific Express Company, was to-day arrested at Denton, Tex., while on his way to New York. The charge on which the arrest was made was the robbery of the express of a package containing about $5,000 last September. He admits the charge. Only $3,000 remains, the rest having been squandered.

Big Union Pacific Contract.

PITTSBURG (Pa.), December 12th.—The big steel rail contract of the Union Pacific, for which Andrew Carnegie and the North Chicago Rolling Company were bidding, has been secured by the Chicago firm. The figure at which it is taken is not exactly known, but is not over $27 per ton—certainly not in excess of $27 50. The contract is for 17,000 tons.

Depew's Friends.

BUFFALO, December 12th.—An interview is published in the News this afternoon with leading men of Buffalo on the subject of Chauncey M. Depew for Minister to England. Politicians, city officials, Supreme Court Judges, bankers, lawyers, physicians, clergymen and merchants are quoted in favor of Depew's appointment.

Actually Afraid of Our Navy.

NEW YORK, December 12th.—Advices from Port-au-Prince say that General Legitim claims to have good reasons for holding the steamer Hay汀 Republic, but doesn't wish to fight for her. He leaves the settlement of the case with the United States Government.

Pardon Refused a Perjurer.

SPRINGFIELD (Ill.), December 12th.—Governor Oglesby today refused to pardon Josh C. Mackin, sentenced to the penitentiary for five years, for perjury committed while testifying before the Grand Jury in reference to election frauds, in which he was supposed to have been particeps criminis.

Two Men Lynched.

KANSAS CITY, December 12th.—It is reported this evening that two men were hanged by vigilantes nine miles south of this city. The report was confirmed later by a call for the Coroner and two coffins. The men were probably horsetieves, but no particulars are at hand to night.

An Insane Mother's Terrible Deed.

NEW YORK, December 12th.—An insane German woman, residing with her husband and two children in a tenant flat in this city, to-night threw her children down the air-shaft and jumped down herself upon the bodies. The children are dead and the mother will die.

Rough on Yankee Smokers.
New York, December 12th.—Word comes from Havana that an English syndicate has bought several of the largest cigar factories and will form a monopoly of all the fine cigars made in Cuba for the European markets, thus shutting out the United State completely.

Two Shocking Deaths.
TRENTON (N. J.), December 12th.—Brakeman John Wharton, while trying to put a tramp off the Pennsylvania Railroad train this morning, fell between the rapidly moving cars, dragging the tramp with him. Both were killed and horribly mangled.

Three Mariners Lost in a Gale.
Norfolk (Va.), December 12th.—The schooner Sis Church, bound from Cape Charles to Norfolk, light, was sunk in the storm on Monday night. Captain Frank Enoch, mate Harris one of the crew, name unknown, were lost.

Postal Crooks on Trial.
Chicago, December 12th.—The trial of Oberkampf and Mack, who will be remembered as having been engaged in the most extensive robbery of letter-boxes ever known, last summer, was begun in the United States Court to-day.

The Situation at Bevier.
Bevier, December 12th.—Officials decline to say what the military will do in the event of an attempt being made by the strikers to erect fortifications, as they threaten. They claim to have lumber coming for that purpose.

The Burlington Dynamite Cases.
Geneva (Ill.), December 12th.—Several witnesses were on the stand to-day in the dynamite case. Alexander Smith, the informer, testified to putting an explosive on the track, under orders from Baureisen.

A Hellish Deed.

A Switchman's Terrible Death.

Serious Charge Against a Doctor.

MISSOURI STATE NEWS.
long-continued suit of David Potheringham against the Adams Express Company for unwarranted imprisonment has been compromised and settled. The company paid the ex-messenger $8,300 and his costs.

Dr. J. A. C. Brown, one of the leading citizens of Pettis County, died at his home in Dresden, a few days ago, of consumption. The deceased was a North Carolinian by birth, served with distinction in the Confederate army and filled many positions of honor and trust in Pettis County. He was about fifty-five years of age and popular with all classes.

Mrs. Lydie C. Jones, wife of Colonel Charles H. Jones, editor of the St. Louis Republic, died recently after a painful illness of long duration, aged forty years. The deceased was an estimable lady, of an amiable and charitable disposition, and her death will be sincerely mourned by her many warm and devoted friends.

The annual election for thirteen directors of the St. Louis Fair Association was held a few days since, and the following gentlemen were chosen: Charles Green, Alvah Mansur, John M. Sellers, L. M. Rumsey, A. B. Ewing, Wm. W. Withnell, John Scullin, W. R. Allen, Richard C. Kerens, Rolla Wells, James Green, Socrates Newman, C. D. McLure.

At least twenty Eastern manufacturers are at present considering removing to or building branch establishments at Kansas City, and promoters who have them in charge are each confident that he will secure the location of the particular factory he is figuring on.

The material and good will of the Sedalia Democrat Newspaper Company was sold at trustee's sale, a few days ago, under four deeds of trust, for $1,000.

The post-office at Mitchellville, Harrison County, has been discontinued; mail to Bethany.

John H. Dorman committed suicide in St. Louis, a few days ago, by shooting himself with a shotgun. He was sixty-nine years of age.

Charles Warner, of Kansas City, made a second attempt recently to commit suicide while at Wichita, Kas., because his wife was unfaithful to him and was living in a disreputable house.

John McCabe, a switchman, employed in the Wabash yards at St. Louis, fell from a car, a few days ago, and sustained severe internal injuries which may prove fatal. McCabe is forty-two years of age and has a wife and several children.

Robert Guerke, Michael Engelkraut and Edward Burke are charged, in a warrant sworn out at St. Louis, with assault to do great bodily harm. They are the three dog-catchers who were accused of handling Willie Maier so brutally. The boy appeared at the Four Courts and swore to the information. He is in a pitiable condition.

The St. Louis Post-Dispatch poor children's Christmas Tree boom is growing to mammoth proportions, the fund being well on the way to $4,000. Prominent citizens have been enlisted in the scheme, and it promises to be one of the most popular charities ever indulged in by the charitable of that city. The children of all classes seem to be enthusiastic over it.

Governor Morehouse has issued a commutation to Lewis Willers, a negro, sentenced from Livingston County in 1884, to the penitentiary for ninety-nine years for murder in the second degree. The sentence is cut down to ten years, with benefits of the three-fourths rule. The sentence was considered unreasonably severe and would have been reduced by the judge of the trial court had not the case been appealed and thus removed from his jurisdiction.

Only four of the Missourians voted for the Direct-Tax bill on its final passage in the House of Representatives at Washington. They were the two Republicans, Wade and Warner, and two Democrats, Mansur and Heard. Four members of the delegation were absent. They were O'Neil, Glover, Stone and Burnes. The others voted against the bill. The amount with which Missouri is credited, and which amount will be returned to the State in the event that the bill becomes a law, is $761,127,33.

Mrs. Haub, living in St. Louis, was washing some clothes in her room, a few days ago, and her son Charles, eighteen months old, was playing on a sofa. She left the room for a few minutes and on returning found the dead body of her baby boy in the tub of water she had just left. It seems that in climbing on the sofa he slipped off and fell into the tub and was drowned before his mother returned.

The bodies of two men were found hanging to a tree at a point near a school-house six miles south of Westport, Jackson County, a few days ago. The supposition is that the bodies were those of horse-thieves who had been lynched by farmers.

In making an estimate of what will be the population of Missouri January 1, 1889, Secretary of State McGrath figures that it will only fall short of 3,000,000 by 250,000. This result is reached by estimating the number of voters in the State at 551,000 and multiplying it by five, which is considered a fair ratio. According to this estimate the population of the State in 1890 will exceed 3,000,000, and the increase in the ten years from 1880 to 1890 will be slightly above 30 per cent. In the estimate for next year he gives St. Louis 450,000, and for 1890 500,000, placing the other large cities in the State as follows: Kansas City, 250,000; St. Joseph, 75,000; Springfield, 50,000, and Hannibal, 25,000.

It may seem very odd that a man can commit suicide while there is a police officer sitting next to his side. Still such was the case in St. Louis, a few evenings since, when a man, supposed to be A. Gansowski, sent a bullet through the center of his head while the ambulance was carrying him en route to the city dispensary, with Police officer Fuqua by his side.

A scene which is not witnessed very frequently occurred in City Counselor Bell's office in St. Louis, a few days ago. It was the destruction by fire of city bonds, which, if signed and executed, would have been worth $72,000. There were 720 bonds in all of the denomination of $100 each. They were left over from the issue of 1886, bearing interest at 3.65 per cent., and were not executed. St. Louis has a ghost sensation. Harry Chapman, one of Sam Jones' converts, who has been serving a sentence in the Jackson County jail for peti larceny, was discharged a few days ago. He was immediately taken before Justice Maybury, charged with being one of the quartette of pickpockets who plied their trade at the Log Cabin about election time. He was bound over to the grand jury.

THE residence of John R. King, of Cookville, Texas, was burned, and King, his wife and six children perished in the flames. The bodies of the eight victims were taken from the ruins and buried in one grave.

COMPLETE returns for Presidential electors in West Virginia, show an average majority for the Cleveland electors on the face of the returns of 536. The vote for the highest electors on each ticket was: Travers (Democrat), 75,588; Pollock (Republican), 75,052.

MISS ALICE BYRUM, a teacher, and Miss Lewis, her pupil, were killed by a train while attempting to walk along a railroad trestle near Alexanders, N. C.

VICE-PRESIDENT-ELECT LEVI P. MORTON and Mrs. Morton arrived at Indianapolis, Ind., on a visit to General Harrison, and were received at the door of the Harrison mansion by the President-elect.

COLOROW, the great chief of the Southern Utes, has died at Ouray Agency, on Green River, Utah, of pneumonia, at the age of seventy. He was the leader in the Meeker massacre and in the Colorow war a year ago.

GOVERNOR JACKSON, of Maryland, telegraphed Secretary Whitney asking for steam launches and Gatling guns from Annapolis to protect the police boat Folly, and United States launches and guns were ordered to Hackett's Point, where the Folly was surrounded by forty piratical oyster dredgers.

THE schooner Sis Church, of New London, Conn., went ashore between Lynn Haven Bay and Ocean View, Va., and the Captain, the mate and two Portuguese sailors were lost.

E. L. HARPER, who stole the funds of the Fidelity Bank to use in grain speculation, and who is in the Penitentiary at Columbus, Ohio, has become a raving maniac.

A MAN from Arizona shot and killed the cashier of the National Bank at San Bernardino, Cal., because he refused to cash a check.

A BOILER explosion in G. W. Turner's cotton gin, near Montgomery, Ala., killed three men. Seven other persons were wounded.

The bodies of two horse thieves, who had probably been lynched by a roving band of vigilantes, were found hanging to a tree near the village of Westport, Mo.

W. T. COLEMAN, the millionaire San Francisco merchant and canner who recently failed for $3,000,000, has settled with his creditors on the basis of sixty per cent. for secured and forty per cent. for unsecured ones. The payments will aggregate $1,180,000.

VICE-PRESIDENT-ELECT MORTON and Mrs. Morton were extended a public reception at Indianapolis, Ind., while on a visit to General Harrison.

LYMAN PUSLEE, a Choctaw, has been executed at Alonka, Indian Territory, for the murder of his brother.

MISS ELIZA McKAY, of Charleston, S. C., owner of the National Hotel, was struck and killed by a train at Banberg, S. C.

MR. WOODS, of Fort Dodge, Iowa, was roasted alive in presence of her six children, her dress having caught fire from a cook stove.

A MAN named McGairn and his niece, Miss Quinlan, while attempting to cross the tracks at Dawson, Neb., were struck by a train and instantly killed.

The trestle work on the Waterworks stand pipe being erected at Stevens Point, Wis., fell, killing four men and seriously wounding two more.

The Georgia House of Representatives has passed a bill appropriating half a million dollars for the common schools of the State.

UNITED STATES Custom House officers captured $20,000 worth of opium which was shipped from Vancouver, British Columbia, and landed at Port Huron, Mich., from a small schooner.

The American Federation of Labor, which has been in session at St. Louis, has adjourned after re-electing Samuel Gompers President. It was decided to institute a general eight-hour movement in January, 1890. Boston will be the next place of meeting.

The body of little Irene, youngest child of Dick Hawes, whose arrest and protection caused the tragedy at Birmingham, Ala., has been found in the lake at that place weighted down with railroad iron. Hawes showed no emotion when informed that the body had been discovered.

Chief-Justice Charles E. Boyle, of Washington Territory, died of pneumonia at Seattle.

The day set for the abolishment of all restrictions against entering Jacksonville, Fla., has passed. The return of those who left there in the early stages of the yellow fever epidemic has been signalized by a big demonstration. The refugees returned by train, boat and private conveyances and afoot.

During the races at St. Londry, La., a family feud which has existed for several years between the migginbothams broke out. As a result of the fight two of the participants were instantly killed and one, who was mortally wounded, died in a few hours. Four others, including an elderly woman, were wounded.

A RAVISHER LYNCHED.
The Scoundered Confesses and Short Work is Made of Him.
DUBLIN, Miss., Aug. 8.—Six miles southeast of this place, a negro name Will Robinson made an assault with intent to outrage the person of a respectable white lady in the upper edge of Tallahatchie, and on the line of Coahoma county, Saturday night last, and would have accomplished the hellish deed but providentially a peddler was lodging there for the night, and hearing her screams ran into the room with a pistol. The negro became frightened and escaped by the window through which he entered the house, leaving his track, by which he was identified. The matter was kept quiet until the following Tuesday, when a posse of men arrested three negroes on the place and carried them into the yard and examined their tracks and found the track made under the window the night of the assault, which had been kept under a box, corresponded perfectly with Robinson's foot, there being a disfigured toe on his left foot.

A meeting was then held and an investigation made. The negro confessed the charges. There having been a case similar to this some weeks previous, in the same neighborhood, the people became very much enraged, and about 100 white and colored people assembled and took the negro to Staton's stretch, Tallahatchie county, this morning, at 10 o'clock, and hung him without law or ceremony.

LYNCHED FOR AN OLD CRIME.
The Murderer of Gen. Grimes Taken from Jail and Killed.
RALLEIGH, N. C., March 12.—A special to the News and Observer from Washington, N. C., says: About 3 o'clock this morning the steamer Beta, on her way to this place, blew a signal to open the draw to the bridge. The bridgekeeper responded, but found an obstruction in the way. The draw could not be opened sufficiently for the steamer to pass. On investigation it was found that there was a rope hanging from a crossbeam of the draw with heavy weight attached. When pulled up a litless body was found at the end of the rope, to which was attached a placard with the inscription "Justice at last."

The proper authorities were promptly notified, and the body was left to dangle till daylight and until a coroner's jury could be emancipated. The body proved to be that of William A. Parker, who was tried for the assassination of Gen. Byran Grimes, some seven or eight years ago. He has been heard to boast of the deed on several occasions when in liquor. It seems that yesterday for drunkenness and disorderly conduct he was consigned to the lockup, a place partitioned off in the rear of the engine-house, with three cells for such cases. An old colored man at night looks after and attends to the wants of the prisoners, he sleeping in an adjoining cell. He deposed at the inquest that about 2 o'clock a.m. he was awakened by a slight noise, and noticed that the light left burning was out, and before he could realize what was the matter he was confronted by at least half a dozen masked men, who told him to keep quiet on pain of death. They approached the cell in which Parker was confined, wrenching off the lock and carried him outside. He was heard to cry out "murder" once or twice. There is no evidence as to who the participants in this transaction are.

Parker, stark and cold, a gag in his mouth, and a rope tight about his neck and fast to the iron rod supporting the bridge draw above. His feet were both a short distance from the water below, and above his head on a placard were written, in a clear, determined hand, these fatd words, "Justice at Last."

It seems that Parker was in town Saturday attending to business in the morning, but later was drinking and boisterous. It is said that he boasted, as he had done several times before, that it was he who killed Gen. Grimes. About 7 o'clock he became so drunk that he was placed in the lock-up, in the rear of fire companies' engine rooms, underneath Town Hall, and Rafe Long, the colored night watch, left in charge. At ten minutes past 2 the street lamps near by were suddenly extinguished, and immediately a dozen or fifteen men, some of them masked, filed in, ordered the keeper to get into a cell and closed the door on him, then broke the lock on Parker's cell and brought him forth to his doom. Intoxicated as he was, or supposing that friends had come to his rescue, he seems to have made no resistance, until he reached the street, when he cried "Murder!" two or three times. Doubtless he was then gaged and carried forward to the place of execution.

—Having investigated the complaint of "Many Farmers," that the authorities of the city of Raleigh discriminate against transient dealers in horses in favor of local dealers, we find that there is no just ground for the complaint. The city tax on dealers in horses is fixed at $25 a year. This tax is paid by the resident and transient dealers alike, and secures a license to carry on such business one year.

—We saw some interesting relics of the olden times at Newbern, among them the old family clock of Governor Tryon. We saw, too, a pair of pants made of home-spun for a man who was born and raised in "that country of malaria, frogs and fever," as some people erroneously call it, which measured 54 inches in length, 56 inches in the waist, and 64 inches in the hip, and being too small for the man, they had never been worn.

—An experienced pomologist having made an examination, informs us that very few of the peaches have thus far been killed. He further informed us that not more than one-fourth of the apricots have been damaged by the cold, and he says it is a fact known to all fruit growers that as long as any apricots escape there is sure to be an ample peach crop. We are glad to hear this report, as some days ago, it was reported that the peaches had been killed in the bud.

—The Wilson Mirror, that pathetic, aesthetic, journalistic marvel of the nineteenth century, which causes you to laugh and weep by alternation, and which is the pet-idol of the feminine gender universal, closed its sixth volume with last week's issue. By reason of its unique and extraordinary style, it is probably better known abroad than any other North Carolina journal. There is just one Wilson Mirror, and it has no imitators.

Public Printer Benedict at Washington, has refused to give the Committee investigating his bureau the names of the persons who informed him of the character of the work performed by certain discharged employees on the ground that the information was given in confidence. The Republican members of the committee have threatened to bring the matter before the House with the view of having the contumacious witness incarcerated for contempt until he divulges.

This man was believed to have been the murderer of Gen. Bryan Grimes, and, indeed, he was arrested and tried for the crime in the year 1880, but was acquited.
