annual session of the North Carolina Medical Society began this morning at Williams's Hall, Fayetteville—Dr. T. D. Haigh, of Fayetteville, presiding, and Dr. Julian E. Baker, of Tarboro', secretary. The attendance is up to the secretary. This afternoon President Haligh delivered the annual address. To-morrow evening the people of the town will give a banquet and ball to the society. On Thursday the society will participate in the memorial-day exercises, and on the evening of that day the annual oration before the society will be delivered.

Near Davidson College lightning struck the warehouse of John Caldwell and burned it with its contents, causing a loss of $1,200.

The municipal election at Durham yesterday was quite exciting. There were three tickets in the field, headed by John F. Freeland, W. J. Christian, and Thomas C. Oakley respectively for mayor. Oakley was the labor candidate, but many of his pledged friends deserted him and voted for Christian, who was elected.

The people of Monroe are greatly excited by the brutal murder of Policeman John Pearce by a negro named Bill Weddington. There was a row at a negro festival, and Pearce arrested the leader in the disturbance and started to the guard-house with him. A mob of negroes gathered and decided that they would rescue the negro who was under arrest. Weddington with a heavy iron bar in his hand was in the rear of Pearce. Frank Thomas, another negro, armed with a bludgeon, cried out, "Kill him!" Whereupon Weddington with one stroke crushed the skull of Pearce, who soon died, never having regained consciousness. Weddington was arrested at once, and Thomas, who had fled to Charlotte, was also captured. Both are in jail at Monroe. Thomas was tried for murder two years ago and got off. Pearce leaves a wife and four children.

The French corvette Brisson has arrived at Wilmington, whose people are showing her officers many courtesies.

It has been found that there are not enough legal signatures to the petition for the local-option election at Charlotte, and the county commissioners have withdrawn the order for the election.

The Federal Court began to-day at Asheville—Judge Dick presiding.

Reports to the Department of Agriculture from Durham and Orange counties state that the wheat and oats crops are being ruined by the prolonged and unusual drought. The same report says the tobacco-plants look well, and that large crops will be planted.

Mr. Hasten Poe, whose sister, Miss Ida Poe, was shot at Carthage by Robert L. McNeill, returned here to-day. He reports that her wound is not at present regarded as dangerous. No tidings of McNeill can be heard. This morning before daylight the town of Carthage, and particularly the house of McNeill's father, was strongly guarded, if having been rumored that McNeill was back in town in hiding. Search for him continued all last night, with the avowed intention of lynching. There is a belief this afternoon that he has after all gone safely away, and is now in Texas or on his way there for refuge.

North Carolina is rather coming towards the front in the matter of lynching. There has not been a legal execution this year, yet there have been five persons lynched. On the 27th of January Matthew Blouat, John Blount, and Patterson Spruill (all colored) were disposed of at Plymouth by his Honor Judge Lynch, and the same judge had another victim at Washington March 12th in the person of a white man, who boasted that he was the assassin of General Bryan Grimes. The last victim at this date is Frazier, who was disposed of at Washington last Saturday night for the murder of Cox. Of the persons sentenced legally to be hanged there have been the following, the commutations being in every case save one to life imprisonment: Charles F. Jones, Newberne; Lucien Rowe, Durham; James Thomas, Hendersonville; Allen McCarter, Statesville, and Daniel Biggs, Wilmington.

The Wake county Grape-Growers' Association met to-day and beard reports. It is discovered that vineyards west of the city and in this township were not hurt by the frosts of late April, while vineyards east of the city have suffered much damage.

Rev. Dr. C. H. Strickland, of Nashville, Tenn., was this evening called to the pastorate of the First Baptist church of this city. He is a very able man and will receive a $3,000 salary.

Captain E. R. Stamps, president of the Board of Directors of the penitentiary, and Mr. W. J. Hieks, warden of that institution, are now in the Blue-Ridge country inspecting the convict quarters in that section. The penitentiary is greatly cramped for funds and may have to remove from railways some of the convicts whose labor has been furnished free.

Major John Gatling, once so prominent as a lawyer, and who died yesterday morning, was buried this afternoon from Christ church, Rev. Dr. M. M. Marshall conducting the services.

The unfortunate white woman who drowned herself some days ago in Robeson county was a native of Robeson county. She ran away from her husband some months ago, and the greater part of the time wandered here and there.

There has been some dispute as to whether the names of the signers of the petition for a local-option election in Barton's-Creek township, Wake county, were or were not those of bona-fide voters, and so the county commissioners have been considering the matter.

The pea crop in the Goldsboro' section is about all picked. It has been quite remunerative. Next week the land now in peas will be planted in corn or cotton.

The Cape-Fear and Yadkin-Valley railroad make a fine showing in the matter of net earnings for the year ended April 30th. They were $31,188 in excess of those during the previous year.

A great revival is in progress in the Baptist church at Fayetteville. There have been many converts.

It is rather noticeable that the Democratic Convention of Cumberland county did not instruct its delegates as to the man they should support for Governor.

Mrs. Rebecca Long's house, in Richmond county, was burned a night or two ago, causing a loss of $1,500, with no insurance. Raleigh is well represented at the session of the Grand Lodge of Independent Order Odd-Fellows, which met at Greensboro' this morning in the hall of Buena Vista lodge. Grand Representatives Charles M. Busbee and C. B. Edwards are present. Captain W. A. Bobbitt, of Oxford, is grand master.

There were elections yesterday at several towns. At Shelby the Democrats were successful and W. L. Damson was reelected mayor. At Newberne the "Coalition party" carried the day. This is the "Reform party," composed of Democrats and the better class of Republicans which figured so extensively in the campaign of 1886. At Goldsboro' the Democrats were again winners, electing eight of the nine aldermen. At Greensboro' John A. Barringer was elected mayor.

Great fires have raged through the forests in Caldwell and Watauga counties, in a district covering some fifty or sixty square miles. The damage is immense. A great deal of the timber burned is chestnut.

Gang of Outlaws Broken Up. Special to the Indianapolis Journal PARKERSBURG, W. Va., Dec. 5.—In the Circuit Court of this county, to-day, Van Wells, Jesse Anderson and William Pease, all of Meigs county, Ohio, found guilty of breaking into and robbing the Ohio River railroad depot and Adams Express office at Believille, W. Va., on the night of Sept. 1 last, were sentenced to five years each in the penitentiary at Moundsville. John Whitehead, also implicated in the same robbery, but who had turned State's evidence, and subsequently withdrew his plea of guilty, was remanded to jail, and will be tried at the next term of court. This is believed to effectually break up a regularly organized band of outlaws, who have been making repeated depredations along the Ohio river in both Ohio and West Virginia. Business Embarrassments.
St. Louis, Dec. 5.—The firm of Eaton, Ginan & Co., of Waco, Tex., was closed, yesterday, by the sheriff, under writs of attachment issued at the instance of the Bank of California, San Francisco, and others. The liabilities are said to be over $100,000. Assets not stated.

BALTIMORE, Dec. 5.—The Baxter Electric Manufacturing and Motor Company, of Baltimore City, yesterday made a deed of trust, for the benefit of creditors, to J. Frank Morrison, trustee. It is understood that the bond will be $100,000. The failure was due to inability to make prompt collections. The firm is said to be solvent.

American Base-Ball Association.

St. Louis, Dec. 5.—The American Association of Base-ball Clubs elected officers to-night. They are: President, secretary and treasurer, Wheeler C. Wikoff, Columbus; vice-president, John W. Speas, Kansas City; chairman, Chris. Von DerAhe, St. Louis; board of directors, Athletics and Columbus in the East, and Cincinnati and Louisville in the West; board of arbitration, Byrne, of Brooklyn; Stern, of Cincinnati; Kranthoff, of Kansas City. Columbus, O., was admitted to the Association in place of Cleveland, resigned to enter the League.

Dakota Statehood Convention.

JAMESTOWN, D. T., Dec. 5.—The North Dakota statehood convention was called to order at 2 P. M., and after some wrangling, ex Gov. Gilbert A. Pierce was elected chairman and delivered an address detailing the claims of Dakota to division and admission. As far as population was concerned, he urged that North Dakota was fully competent for statehood. Her crops, her capital, her permanent improvements, her educational progress surpassed those of many States long since admitted. He dwelt on the necessity of harmony when working to secure early action.

The Philadelphia Natural-Gas Company.

PITTSBURG, Dec. 5.—At a meeting of the stockholders of the Philadelphia Natural-gas Company, to-day, a resolution was adopted authorizing the issue of $2,500,000 bonds, to be used in the extension of the plant. The liabilities of the company are $1,300,000, and it is the intention to issue $1,500,000 of the bonds immediately to pay off this debt. The other million will be held in reserve. The meeting was largely attended, almost the entire capital stock of $7,500,000 being represented.

Driven Away Because He Was Elected.

CANTON, O., Dec. 5.—A colored man, who has been in Canton and vicinity for the past few days, tells a strange story. He says he was elected constable in a country district twenty miles from Atlanta, Ga., on Nov. 6. Next day he received warning from a vigilance committee that no "niggers" could hold office, and that he must leave or be hanged. He left. The man, who is intelligent, says he worked his way North, and gives his name as Williams.
